evidence: `.github/workflows/cost-index-refresh.yml` lines 79-83: if `/tmp/ci-artifact.json` is absent the step prints `No artifact written (0 points composed) — keeping last-good data; see fetch log.` and `exit 0` — a green job. Line 62-66 does the same when no API keys are set. The Commit step then finds nothing staged and exits cleanly. Empirically the workflow IS running (`data(cost-index): measured read 2026-08-05`, `2026-08-03` bot commits) and still 26 of 100 series are frozen 58–88 days, 8 of them newly frozen since the board was written on 2026-07-31 (`yellow-squash` 88d, `cherry-tomato` 84d, `collard-greens` 80d, `napa-cabbage` 80d, `artichoke` 78d, `butter-lettuce` 77d, `green-beans` 72d, `acorn-squash` 60d — all USDA-AMS produce, all flagged STALE LEVEL ANCHOR). Board open item 8 attributes 15 frozen feeds to a NOAA outage; these eight are not NOAA and are new.
impact: The frozen roster nearly doubled in six days while every workflow ran green and every deploy-time freshness gate read "fresh". The public Cost Index — the citable, CC0-licensed asset the whole funnel rests on — is publishing composite reads whose underlying prints are ten weeks old, and `basket.asOf` is dated by two frozen basket contributors (`shrimp`, `vegetable-oil`, plus `salmon-fillet` in the known-latent set).
rec: Make partial failure loud without making it blocking: after the fetch, have the workflow run `check-cost-index-series-freshness.mjs` and, if the UNEXPECTED count has GROWN versus the previous run, fail the job (the issue-opening pattern from `freshness-heartbeat.yml` already exists and can be copied). Then run the one diagnostic the board already specifies — `node scripts/fetch-cost-index-sources.mjs --live --out /tmp/ci.json` on the Mac — and read the `source family FAILED` block for the produce feeds, which are AMS, not NOAA.

title: The warrant canary is 88 days stale, 3 monthly cycles overdue, has no gate, and the live privacy policy links to a URL that does not exist
evidence: Muntin-Invoice-Decoder/docs/warrant-canary.md line 3: '**Last updated and signed:** 2026-05-10' — 88 days ago. Its own Cadence section: 'This statement is updated on the **first day of each calendar month**. The next scheduled update is **2026-06-01**.' Three scheduled updates (06-01, 07-01, 08-01) have been missed. The same document states: 'If the warrant canary disappears or stops being updated on schedule, draw your own conclusions.' No gate exists: `grep -rln canary scripts/ .github/workflows/` returns NOTHING, and check-gate-coverage.mjs reports '39 check scripts — 39 run by CI, 0 documented as deliberately unwired' — a gate never written cannot be flagged unwired. Meanwhile scripts/check-subprocessor-freshness.mjs DOES enforce a 30-day window and passes ('6 active rows passed the 30-day freshness check'). Worse, it is unpublishable: `ls apps/web/app/(marketing)/legal/` returns dpia, privacy, ropa, terms, transparency — there is no warrant-canary route, and app/(marketing)/legal/transparency/page.tsx:55 only globs `/^transparency-\d{4}q[1-4]\.md$/`, so no route can ever serve this file. Yet apps/web/lib/legal-content.generated.ts:142-143 (published at /legal/privacy) reads 'publish a warrant canary at [docs/warrant-canary.md](./warrant-canary.md)', repeated at :259-260, :280-281, :762, :892, :915 across the DPA and security copy.
impact: The company's single differentiator is privacy-by-construction, and the one artifact whose entire function is to decay visibly has decayed invisibly. A reader of the live privacy policy is told a warrant canary is published, clicks a relative link that 404s, and — if they found the file — would read a statement 3 cycles past its self-declared cadence, which by the document's own instruction means 'draw your own conclusions.' Every CI gate in the repo is green while this is true. This is the audit's own thesis in its purest form, and the domain auditor spent 11 findings on build plumbing without opening it.
rec: Three steps, small. (1) Re-sign docs/warrant-canary.md today and correct the 'next scheduled update' date. (2) Write scripts/check-warrant-canary-fresh.mjs on the exact model of check-subprocessor-freshness.mjs — parse 'Last updated and signed' and fail past 35 days — and wire it into ci.yml plus the cost-index-snapshot-watch.yml Monday cron in the same commit. (3) Either add a /legal/warrant-canary route rendering the markdown (the transparency page's renderer is 20 lines away from doing it) or, if publishing it is not intended before GA, strike the six claims from legal-content.generated.ts. Do not leave the copy promising something no URL serves.

title: check-image-formats passes by asserting a property of zero items, is warn-only, and is listed in CLAUDE.md as a live LCP guard
evidence:
`node scripts/check-image-formats.mjs` prints 'Image formats: 0 hero (s) across 1364 HTML file(s); all wrapped with /WebP source.' — a success sentence about an empty set. Its heuristic (header lines 8-11) matches an image only if it sits inside a `
` whose class contains 'hero' or the `` itself has a hero class; that matches none of the site's 722 `` tags (confirmed against check-lazy-images and check-image-dimensions, which both scan 722 real tags and are genuinely doing work). Line 16 of the header: 'WARN_ONLY by default; flip after the existing tree is cleaned' — and it is the only check-*.mjs in the repo with WARN_ONLY set true. The companion injector is equally inert: scripts/inject-picture-tags.mjs reports '0 tag(s) across 0 page(s) would be wrapped' because it only wraps a raster src when both `.avif` and `.webp` siblings already exist (siblingExists, lines 75-86). Site-wide there are 42 raster `` tags and exactly 2 .avif and 2 .webp files in the whole repo. CLAUDE.md's Key gates section lists check-image-formats alongside check-image-dimensions and check-lazy-images as 'CLS / LCP guards'.
impact: CLAUDE.md — the document a fresh context reads first — presents three working performance guards. Two work; the third can never fail, would not fail if it could, and covers a real deficit (40 of 42 raster images ship with no modern-format alternative on a content site whose funnel depends on page speed). The auditor's own metric — '~89% of gates inspect committed text and structure' — undercounts the problem, because this gate does not merely inspect structure, it inspects nothing and prints a promise.
rec: Delete the hero heuristic and scope the gate to what actually exists: fail (not warn) on any `` with a raster src that has no `` wrapper AND no avif/webp sibling, with a dated HISTORICAL_WAIVERS list for the current 40 so it lands green. Then either generate the siblings or accept the debt explicitly. If neither is worth founder time, delete the gate and strike it from CLAUDE.md's Key gates list — a gate documented as protection and incapable of protecting is worse than no gate, which is this repo's own stated position on unwired gates.

title: check-cross-repo-seams does not cover the cross-repo seam that has now broken twice
evidence: Muntin-Invoice-Decoder/scripts/check-cross-repo-seams.mjs passes with: '✓ cross-repo seams: window links attributed (?source=ledger); shared business @id + contact intact'. That is its entire scope — outbound link attribution and shared JSON-LD identity. The actual load-bearing cross-repo dependency is the vendoring path: apps/api/scripts/vendor-cost-pressure.mjs:38,43 and its cost-index sibling read `../../../../potentially-profitable/data/*.json` from a checkout that no workflow in either repo ever produces. That seam went dark for 42 days in production (CLAUDE.md, 'Cost-Index snapshot refresh CLOSED 2026-07-30'), and its twin is 4 days from going dark again today (check-cost-pressure-snapshot-fresh EXIT=1, asOf 2026-07-20, 21d cliff). The gate that carries the name 'cross-repo seams' cannot see either.
impact: A founder scanning green CI sees a gate literally named for this risk class reporting clean, which is active misdirection rather than a mere gap. The two snapshot-freshness gates that DO catch it are named for data staleness, not for the seam, so the naming points attention away from the failure mode. This is why the same defect recurred on the sibling feature seven days after being closed on the first.
rec: Either rename the existing gate to what it checks (check-cross-repo-links) and add a real seam gate, or extend it: assert that every path in either repo resolving outside its own root is (a) produced by a named workflow, or (b) listed in a MANUAL registry with who runs it and when it drifts — the exact contract check-idem-coverage already enforces on builders. Board open item 9 (the cross-repo PAT) is the standing fix; until it is minted, the registry entry is the honest substitute.

title: The published Q2 transparency report is still marked 'partial, final at 2026-07-01' — 36 days past its own deadline — on a live public route with no gate
evidence: Muntin-Invoice-Decoder/docs/transparency-2026q2.md lines 3-12: '> **Partial — final report at 2026-07-01.** This document covers the partial quarter window 2026-04-01 through 2026-05-11 ... the final Q2 2026 report will replace the partial figures below.' Today is 2026-08-06. The file is served publicly: apps/web/app/(marketing)/legal/transparency/[quarter]/page.tsx:73 reads `docs/transparency-${quarter}.md` and the index at page.tsx:55 lists every matching file. The generating cron IS registered — apps/api/wrangler.toml:260 includes `0 6 1 1,4,7,10 *` and src/index.ts:19 imports runQuarterlyTransparency — so the machine half ran on 2026-07-01 and wrote to R2, but the hand-authored markdown twin (which is what the public page actually renders) was never replaced. No check script references transparency-*.md staleness; check-subprocessor-freshness and check-security-events do not cover it.
impact: Live public page tells a reader it is provisional and names a date five weeks in the past, on the same legal surface as the missing warrant canary. Two of the three artifacts on /legal that exist to demonstrate the company keeps its own schedule are visibly past schedule. For a product sold on 'it holds a number back rather than print a guess', publishing a report that announces its own obsolescence is the credibility inverse.
rec: Publish the final Q2 rollup from the R2 artifact the cron already wrote, and add a one-rule gate: any docs/transparency-*.md containing a 'final report at <date>' banner whose date has passed fails CI. Five lines, same shape as check-kpi-doc.mjs's _lastReviewed rule.

title: freshness-heartbeat.yml's header claims ~16 time-decay gates; the repo contains 10 and the roster runs 7
evidence: .github/workflows/freshness-heartbeat.yml line 5: 'This repo has ~16 gates that measure TIME rather than correctness'. I swept every scripts/check-*.mjs for `Date.now()` or `new Date()`: exactly 10 match. The roster at lines 66-72 runs 7 of them. The 3 time-aware gates outside the roster that matter are check-cost-index-series-freshness (the only gate that can see a single dead feed — the auditor caught this one), check-cost-index-sync (owner of the 120-day POINT_STALE_DAYS cliff that will drop ingredients), and check-content-guardrails. I ran all 7 roster gates: every one exits 0 today, including check-kpi-doc, which reports `_lastReviewed=2026-06-17 (51d old)` against a STALE_DAYS=90 threshold — so the roster is fully green while 26 of 100 price series are frozen 58-88 days and yellow-squash is 33 days from the sync cliff on a level anchor from 2026-05-11 (check-cost-index-sync.mjs:66 flags `stale-level` if ANY provenance leg exceeds the cliff, via `.some()`).
impact: The workflow's own header is the document a future reader trusts to know what the weekly alarm covers, and it overstates coverage by roughly 60%. The concrete consequence is the one the auditor identified: the Saturday heartbeat cannot see a dead feed or an approaching cliff, so the alarm built for absence is blind to the two absences currently live.
rec: Correct the header count to the real number, and add both check-cost-index-series-freshness and check-cost-index-sync to the GATES list. Series-freshness warns by default so it will not red the job on day one; that is the honest promotion path its own header describes. Also fix check-kpi-doc.mjs:37, which tells the operator to 'Re-examine the 5 KPIs' while data/kpis.json holds 4.

title: Any authenticated member of any role can erase the entire workspace and rewrite its audit chain
effort: 2 hours
evidence: apps/api/src/routes/erasure.ts:62 applies `erasure.use("*", requireAuth)` and nothing else — grep for owner/role in that file returns only two comments (:19, :177), no check. `POST /v1/erasure` (:66) accepts any valid session plus the literal string "delete my workspace", then calls `sessions.revokeAllForOrg` and `tombstoneAuditChainForOrg` (:126). That tombstone primitive (lib/audit.ts:306, implemented at lib/audit-d1.ts:180-214) walks every audit row and rewrites target_ref, prev_hash AND event_hash in a cascade so `verifyChain` stays green afterwards. The route is mounted at index.ts:294 with only the global csrf() middleware at :162.
impact: A `read_only` invitee — the role whose entire purpose is to see and change nothing — can permanently destroy a customer's ledger and simultaneously overwrite the audit record that would show who did it. For a bookkeeping product sold to restaurants that invite staff and outside accountants, this is a single-request, one-disgruntled-employee company-ending event, and it converts the DPA's audit-integrity commitments (docs/dpa.md §10.2) into a promise the code cannot keep.
rec: Add `requireRole("owner")` to the erasure sub-app in the same commit as reading this. It is a one-line change against an already-audited middleware (middleware/require-role.ts) that fail-closes to 503 on a degraded lookup. Add a route test asserting staff and read_only both get 403. While there, fix the bare `catch {}` at erasure.ts:110-116 that swallows the erasure audit write (ground-truth-pack §3.7, open since 2026-06-07).
note: The authorization gap reproduces exactly: erasure.ts:62 is `erasure.use("*", requireAuth)` and nothing else; the only role words in the file are comments; audit-d1.ts:180-214 does cascade prev_hash + event_hash so verifyChain stays green (and audit.ts:317's docstring saying 'prev_hash is unchanged' is genuinely wrong). But the IMPACT is misstated twice. (1) The route destroys no ledger: erasure.ts imports sessions/passkeys/deks/memberships/identity-key/users stores and NO documents or extractions store; nothing in it schedules deletion; the reaper (scheduled/retention-reaper.ts) is retention-driven and only deletes the R2 object + stamps r2_purged_at — it never deletes a Neon row. The real harm is irreversible audit-chain rewriting plus org-wide session revocation. (2) The 'any read_only invitee' precondition is unreachable today: members.ts:194-207 hard-requires an ACTIVE Stripe subscription before an invite can be minted, and no org has one during the free beta, so a second membership row cannot be created. erasure.test.ts (515 lines) contains no role assertion, confirming nothing enforces it.

title: The permission model is sold in the UI and enforced on 1 of 69 API route files
effort: 2 weeks (1 day for the destructive subset)
evidence: `requireRole(` appears in exactly two places outside its own definition and tests: apps/api/src/routes/billing.ts:128 and :221. Counting every form of role check (requireRole, assertOwner, membership.role, isOwner), 8 of 69 route files gate anything. The 61 that do not include exports.ts (`GET /v1/exports/csv` at :54 — the whole ledger), documents.ts, extractions.ts, integrations/posting.ts and integrations/bulk-post.ts (posting bills to QuickBooks), document-deks.ts (DELETE /:document_id/wrapped-dek at :393 permanently orphans an encrypted document), erasure.ts, and inventory.ts. The four roles owner|staff|accountant|read_only are defined and invitable (routes/members.ts:88). STATUS-v6.md:34 recorded "roles stored but unenforced" months ago; it is still true on 2026-08-06.
impact: Every member of a workspace is effectively an owner. A restaurant that invites a line cook to snap invoices has given that person the ability to export the full purchase ledger, delete documents, and push bills into the owner's QuickBooks. Once the accountant tier is sold on the strength of scoped access, shipping a UI that displays roles the API ignores is a misrepresentation, not just a gap — and it is the exact class of finding a first enterprise-deal security questionnaire asks about directly.
rec: Write the route x role matrix once (69 rows, half an afternoon), then apply `requireRole(...)` route-group by route-group starting with the destructive and exfiltrating verbs: erasure, document-deks DELETE, exports, documents delete/bulk-review, integrations posting. Then add a gate in the shape this company already builds well: a script that enumerates mounted routes and fails CI on any authenticated non-GET route absent from an explicit role registry — so the next route cannot ship silently ungated.
note: Reproduced: `requireRole(` appears only at billing.ts:128 and :221 outside middleware/require-role.ts and its tests; 8 of 69 route files contain any role check (accountant-handoffs, billing, bookkeeper, charge-mappings, gl-rules, locations, members, statement-reconciliations). exports.ts:52 mounts `requireAuth` only; document-deks DELETE /:document_id/wrapped-dek (document-deks.ts:393) is confirm-gated but not role-gated. require-role.ts is well-written and fail-closed (503 on lookup throw). Severity corrected down one step for the same reason as above: with invites gated on an active subscription that no org has, every member is today the owner by construction, so this is a pre-GA blocker rather than a live exposure — which is what the auditor's own last sentence concedes.

title: The documents table — and 7 other org-scoped tables — have no row-level security, and no gate would catch the next one
effort: 3 days
evidence: Parsing all 59 migrations: 50 tables created, 8 org-scoped ones carry no ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY — `documents` and `vendors` (0001), `org_categories` + `org_invoice_categories` (0027), `org_budgets` + `org_budget_history` (0028), `vendor_id_map` (0053), and `community_templates` (0013, intentionally pooled). 0015_rls_data_plane.sql:47-58 states the deferral explicitly: the reaper's global sweep sets no GUC, so fail-closed RLS would break purging, and "enabling documents RLS requires the reaper to connect under a BYPASSRLS Postgres role… tracked in runbooks/neon-data-plane.md as an operator follow-up." That follow-up has not happened across the 42 migrations since. The only boundary today is the hand-written `org_id = $1` predicate in NeonDocumentsStore, which is consistently applied (documents-store.ts:575-800) — and lib/integration-attach.ts:64 already reaches R2 with `env.DOCUMENTS.get(document.r2_key)` outside the tenant broker. scripts/check-view-rls.mjs, the only RLS gate, checks CREATE VIEW statements from migration 0039 onward and says nothing about tables.
impact: The documents table holds every customer's r2_key, sha256, org_id and owner — the index to every invoice image in the system. A single forgotten predicate in one future query is a cross-tenant read of the whole customer base, with no second wall and no test that would notice. For a privacy-architected product, one tenant leak is the end of the positioning and probably the company.
rec: Two moves. (1) Provision the reaper's BYPASSRLS role (a Neon console + DATABASE_URL_REAPER change, already designed in 0015's header) and then enable RLS on documents and vendors — this is the migration the repo has been describing for three months. (2) Build the missing gate: a script that parses every migration, and for each CREATE TABLE containing an org_id column asserts a matching ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY + policy, with a dated ALLOW list for deliberate exceptions like community_templates. That gate is worth more than the migration, because it makes the property permanent.
note: I re-derived the list independently by parsing all 59 files in infra/postgres/migrations: 50 CREATE TABLEs, 38 with ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and exactly the 8 org-scoped tables the report names have none — documents, vendors (0001), org_categories, org_invoice_categories (0027), org_budgets, org_budget_history (0028), vendor_id_map (0053), community_templates (0013). 0015_rls_data_plane.sql:46-57 states the documents deferral and its reaper/BYPASSRLS reason verbatim. One correction the report understates: 0015 documents only TWO deferrals (documents, line_item_keys — and line_item_keys got RLS in 0016). The other six are silent omissions with no recorded reasoning at all, which is the worse half of the finding and is not called out.

title: The 24-hour deletion promise is contractual, unverified in production, and has no arming gate
effort: 1 day
evidence: docs/privacy-policy.md:164 and :296 promise "policy default 24h after extraction… enforced by the retention reaper (being enabled)". The reaper only runs if `env.RETENTION_REAPER_ENABLED === "true"` (index.ts:668) and only deletes if DRYRUN is not true (:669). docs/security/ground-truth-pack.md §3.1 records the 2026-06-08 operator check: both secrets are PRESENT but their VALUES are unreadable via wrangler, so the effective state is unknown; the recommended fix ("gate the arming flags") was never built — scripts/check-wrangler-prod-config.mjs gates 7 vars and none of them are arming flags. Separately, `GET /v1/posture` reports `orgs.retention_seconds` straight from the orgs row (routes/posture.ts:143-166) with no reference to whether the reaper runs. For every non-enrolled user (E2EE is opt-in, default off), the plaintext original sits in R2 until that unverified cron deletes it.
impact: A privacy claim in the published privacy policy and the DPA that the company cannot demonstrate is running, plus a customer-facing posture endpoint that will happily assert "24h retention" while nothing is deleting. If a customer or regulator asks for evidence of enforcement, the honest answer today is "we do not know." That answer is survivable pre-revenue and expensive post-revenue.
rec: One `wrangler tail muntin-api` session to read the next `retention_reaper.tick` log and settle it (r2_purged_count = armed, would_purge = dry-run, disabled_in_prod = off). Then build the arming gate: a deploy-time check that asserts the flag values, and change /v1/posture to report enforced-vs-policy as two distinct fields so the pill cannot claim a promise that isn't running.
note: The arming facts reproduce (index.ts:668-669 gate on RETENTION_REAPER_ENABLED/DRYRUN; neither flag is in wrangler.toml). But the report overstates the silence: lib/retention-reaper-disabled-event.ts + index.ts:681-683 already emit a dedicated high-visibility 'disabled in prod' event distinct from the noisy skip log, and erasure.ts:147-154 already degrades the customer-facing copy when the flag is off — the code is more honest than 'no gate exists' implies. The report also misses the larger defect sitting in the same file: even fully ARMED, the reaper deletes only the R2 object and stamps r2_purged_at (retention-reaper.ts:120-260, documents-store markR2Purged). No Neon row is ever deleted by any automated path, so the privacy-policy 'deletion' promise is narrower than either the doc or this finding assumes.

title: E2EE is shipped but opt-in and default-off — and the claims registry instructs writers to state it unconditionally
effort: 2 hours
evidence: Resolving the contradiction in the code: STATUS-v6.md:43-45 ("DEK/UMK uncalled, R2 stores plaintext, recovery-crypto parked off-tree") is STALE. The encrypt seam is live at apps/api/src/lib/queue.ts:1227-1320 (mintDek -> aesEncrypt with document_id as AAD -> wrapToPublicKey -> r2Put .enc -> delete plaintext), packages/recovery-crypto ships Argon2id + X25519, and the enrollment ceremony is reachable at apps/web/app/(product)/settings/security (EncryptCard rendered at page.tsx:566). BUT queue.ts:1259-1272 skips encryption entirely when the owner has no enrolled identity key, and enrollment defaults to `not_enrolled`. The plaintext also transits docling on Fly by design (threat-model.md #1). docs/marketing-claims.md moves "end-to-end encrypted / a key only you hold" to the ✅ list with the instruction: "Keep the present-tense E2EE copy ('a key only you hold') everywhere — do not soften it." The shipped product copy is actually honest and correctly conditional (apps/web/lib/copy.ts:752, :2211 "You can also turn on your own lock"; the vs/* pages say "read once on our infrastructure… you can then turn on a lock"), and I found no unqualified E2EE claim on the storefront. The demo string at copy.ts:3749 ("Your files are locked with a key only you hold") is the one exception, and marketing-claims.md itself flags it as live exposure #3.
impact: The registry is the loaded gun, not the copy. It is the document a future writer (or a future agent) consults, and it currently authorises an unconditional present-tense E2EE claim for a feature that is off for every user who has not completed a 12-word ceremony, on a system where the server reads the plaintext by design. An unconditional "end-to-end encrypted" claim on a paid product is an FTC-deceptive-practices shape and the single easiest thing for a competitor or journalist to falsify.
rec: Edit docs/marketing-claims.md: replace the "do not soften it" instruction with the actual conditional — "opt-in per user; scoped to the stored document image; the extraction pass reads plaintext server-side." Drop the term "end-to-end encrypted" in favour of the mechanism the copy already uses ("a lock only your recovery phrase opens"), which is both accurate and stronger. Fix the demo string at copy.ts:3749 + its ES twin. Separately, correct STATUS-v6.md:43-45, which now understates what shipped.
note: The code half reproduces: the encrypt seam is live at lib/queue.ts:1227-1300 (findForOrg idempotency check -> getOwnerForOrg -> findPublicKeyForOrgUser -> mintDek/aesEncrypt/wrapToPublicKey), it is genuinely skipped when the owner has no identity key (:1245-1272), and the queue consumer is the real path (ingest.ts:399 enqueues, INGEST_QUEUE is bound in wrangler.toml:274-294). STATUS-v6 is indeed stale. But the registry is not the unqualified instruction the finding describes: docs/marketing-claims.md:43 already scopes the claim ('the structured ledger remains server-readable by design — scope the lock to the document image, as the copy already does') and :58 already flags the demo string as live exposure #3. The one thing genuinely missing from the registry is 'opt-in, default-off' — a real but much narrower edit than 'the loaded gun'.

title: Three fail-open paths catalogued 60 days ago are all still open, and the rate-limiter's promised alert does not exist
effort: 4 hours
evidence: apps/api/src/middleware/rate-limit.ts:120 fails open when the binding is missing with the comment "The structured log lets BetterStack alert on 'rate-limit binding missing in prod'"; :134 fails open on a binding error with "The same structured log captures the error." The file contains ZERO `log(` calls — I counted. Both branches return `{allowed:true}`, indistinguishable from a real allow, producing no signal at all. apps/api/src/middleware/require-auth.ts:173-193 catches any membership-lookup error and honors the JWT org claim — a fail-open, asymmetric with require-role.ts:81 which returns 503 on the same condition. All three are ground-truth-pack §3 items 2 and 3, dated 2026-06-07: 60 days open.
impact: The company's own security doctrine is fail-closed, and the three places it is violated are the ones where a failure is invisible. A rate-limit binding outage silently removes the only abuse control on the ingest path — the surface that costs real money per request (Fly machines, R2 writes) — and nobody finds out. This is small in isolation and important as a signal: the ground-truth pack found these, wrote the fix, and nothing moved, which means the security review loop is currently a documentation loop.
rec: Wire `log(env, {event:"ratelimit.fail_open", level:"error", fields:{reason}})` into both branches of probe() — 20 minutes — and either delete the comments' claim or make it true. Flip require-auth's D1-*error* branch (as distinct from "no row") to 503 now that the membership backfill is done. Then add a line to the posture scorecard's cadence: any §3 item open two consecutive cycles gets escalated or explicitly accepted with a date.
note: Reproduced precisely: middleware/rate-limit.ts contains zero `log(` calls and does not import the logger, while probe() at :120 and :134 both return {allowed:true} citing a structured log that does not exist. require-auth.ts:173-193 does catch the membership-lookup error and honor the JWT org claim, asymmetric with require-role.ts:81. Worth adding: the fail-open is load-bearing for the demo path — demo-extract.ts routes its per-ASN cap through the same probe(), so a missing INGEST_RATELIMIT binding silently removes the abuse control on the one endpoint that spends money per request. Staleness math checks out (2026-06-07 to 2026-08-06 = 60 days).

title: The deploy pipeline is a stub, so the image signing the threat model relies on does not exist and no deploy is recorded
effort: 1 day (or 30 min for the honesty + free controls)
evidence: .github/workflows/deploy.yml:72-96 — every one of the four targets (api/docling/extract/web) runs `echo "TODO(B-priv-6): wire wrangler deploy after cosign signing pipeline lands"`. The audit step at :98-103 is likewise `echo "TODO: POST /v1/audit/deploys after the route lands"`. Meanwhile docs/threat-model.md #1 names "pip-audit on every CI run + cosign-signed images" as the mitigation for the docling RCE residual risk — pip-audit is real (ci.yml:695), cosign is not. There is no .github/dependabot.yml and no gitleaks/trufflehog anywhere (ground-truth-pack §3.5, still open).
impact: Every production deploy is a manual wrangler/flyctl invocation from one laptop, unsigned, unrecorded, unreviewable. The blast radius of that laptop is the whole company: it holds the JWT_SECRET, the chain-head Ed25519 private key, DATABASE_URL, and the R2 credentials. The threat model tells a customer (it is deliberately public) about a defense that is not there — which is worse than disclosing the gap, because pen-test-prep.md hands that document to a paid tester as ground truth.
rec: Cheapest honest fix first: edit threat-model.md #1 residual risk to say "pip-audit on every CI run; image signing is planned, not shipped" — 10 minutes, and it removes a false public claim. Then decide deliberately whether cosign is worth 3 days for a one-person company (it probably is not yet) and, if not, delete the stubbed deploy.yml rather than leaving a workflow that looks like a pipeline. What IS worth doing now: enable GitHub secret-scanning push protection and add a dependabot.yml — both are ~15 minutes and cover the git-history gap the scorecard has flagged since June.
note: Reproduced at .github/workflows/deploy.yml:72-96 — all four targets echo 'TODO(B-priv-6)' and the audit step at :98-103 likewise. Additional evidence the report missed in the same 30 lines: the web target's commented-out command is `vercel deploy --prod`, while CLAUDE.md and package scripts say apps/web deploys to Cloudflare via OpenNext — the stub is not merely unwired, it documents a hosting decision that has since been reversed.

title: Contractual 24h/72h breach clocks against a never-rehearsed, one-person, second-job on-call
effort: 1 day for the drill; the DPA edit needs counsel
evidence: runbooks/incident-response.md header table: "Last drill: Not yet executed | Elapsed: n/a | Next drill: First Friday after MVP private beta." The on-call section: "Sprint 0: founder is sole on-call. Once paid GA lands, contractor backup is engaged"; "Pager: BetterStack… Both are set up in BetterStack on first day of paid beta" — i.e. not set up. The P1 SLA is 15 minutes. docs/dpa.md §10.1 commits to GDPR Art. 33 notification within 72 hours of awareness, and §10.2 adds a separate binding 24-hour clock for integrity events including a broken audit chain ("the 24-hour clock is the binding earlier deadline"). The operator works a full-time front-of-house shift at a restaurant; a 15-minute acknowledgment during service is not a thing that can happen.
impact: Nothing is exposed today because there are no customers. On the first paid signup, a legally binding notification clock starts running against a response capability that has never been tested and a pager that has never been configured — and "we did not notice for four days because I was on the floor" is the kind of fact that turns a small incident into a regulatory and reputational one. This is the domain's clearest example of a founder-constraint problem rather than an engineering problem.
rec: Before the first paid customer, do two things. (1) Run the drill once and stamp the table — even a 45-minute tabletop against a fake P1 changes the runbook from aspiration to rehearsed, and will surface the missing BetterStack config for free. (2) Renegotiate the DPA clocks against reality: a 24-hour integrity-event commitment written for a staffed team should become 72 hours aligned with Art. 33, or the contractor backup has to be real and paid before GA. Do not launch paid with §10.2 as written.
note: runbooks/incident-response.md:7-9 header table reads 'Not yet executed | n/a | First Friday after MVP private beta'; the P1 first-response SLA is 15 minutes; docs/dpa.md:225 commits to Art. 33 72 hours and :235-263 adds the separate binding 24-hour chain-integrity clock ('the 24-hour clock is the binding earlier deadline'). All quoted accurately. This is the one finding in the report whose severity is if anything understated relative to the founder constraint, though it correctly notes nothing is exposed pre-revenue.

title: The audit chain is tamper-evident against a database attacker and ceremonial against an operator compromise
effort: 1 day
evidence: lib/audit.ts:162 hashes events with unkeyed SHA-256 over (id, org_id, actor_id, action, target_kind, target_ref, prev_hash, ts) — recomputable by anyone with write access. The external anchor is the 6h Ed25519 chain-head canary, whose signing key (CHAIN_HEAD_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY), whose R2 publication bucket, and whose D1 chain all live in the same Cloudflare account; the published pubkey at docs/transparency.md:57 is real and the key ceremony was genuinely self-corrected on 2026-05-15 (the correction log there is a credit to the design). But lib/audit-d1.ts:180-214 `tombstoneForOrg` is a supported, in-product, full-chain rewrite that cascades prev_hash and recomputes every event_hash so that verifyChain returns green afterwards — reachable by any authenticated member per the erasure finding. Also, the docstring at lib/audit.ts:317 states "prev_hash is unchanged; we only rewrite target_ref + event_hash," which the D1 implementation contradicts — docs and code disagree about a load-bearing property of the integrity primitive.
impact: "Every change is logged; you can read the chain yourself" (docs/marketing-claims.md ✅ row) is true against the threat of a DBA editing rows, and not true against the threat most customers imagine, which is the operator. A green verifyChain proves nothing on its own because a rewrite that produces a green verifyChain is a shipped feature. This does not make the claim false — the canary is a real commitment — but it makes it narrower than it reads, and the 6h publication window plus same-account storage bounds it further.
rec: Fix the wrong docstring at audit.ts:317 today (a future reader will trust it and break the chain). Then either (a) narrow the public claim to what the canary actually anchors — "we publish a signed head every 6 hours off the chain; if we rewrote history the head stops matching" — or (b) make it genuinely external for near-zero cost by also pushing each signed head to a second, differently-owned surface (a commit in the public storefront repo, or a free public timestamping service). Option (b) is a few hours and converts the strongest privacy differentiator from a promise into a proof.

title: The storefront holds customer PII behind a single-email, unrevocable, 30-day cookie — and the documented cross-repo SSO was never built
effort: 1 day
evidence: The storefront is a 9,196-line single-file Worker (src/worker.js) with its own auth: src/lib/auth.js:20 states plainly "Cons: cannot revoke a stolen session before 30-day expiry," and getSessionFromRequest (:293) does a signature+exp check with no revocation lookup. Admin access is `_requireAdminSession` (worker.js:6075): the session email must equal `env.NOTIFY_EMAIL`, which is a plaintext [vars] value in wrangler.jsonc:198 (don@muntin.digital). That gate protects 12 admin endpoints including /api/admin/window/thread and /api/admin/submissions/list — the founder's inbox of customer messages and form submissions. There is no passkey or second factor on this surface (passkeys exist only in the product repo). Separately, docs/auth-integration.md:145 describes a shared JWT_SECRET giving bidirectional SSO across both Workers; the storefront implements nothing of the kind (it uses AUTH_COOKIE_SECRET + an `md_session` 2-part HMAC token, not the API's 3-part JWT), yet apps/api/wrangler.toml still sets SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN = "muntin.digital", scoping the product session cookie to every subdomain for an integration that does not exist.
impact: The lower-security half of the estate holds real customer PII (inbound messages, submissions) behind a magic-link-only, unrevocable, month-long cookie with a publicly known admin identity. If that cookie is captured, there is no revoke — the documented remedy is to wait 30 days or rotate AUTH_COOKIE_SECRET and log everyone out. And the product's session cookie is broadened to the whole apex to serve a design nobody shipped, which means any subdomain compromise (status.*, a future preview deploy) sees it.
rec: Three small things: add a KV revocation check keyed on the existing `jti` in the storefront cookie (the format already carries it — auth.js:17 says so); cut the admin session TTL to hours rather than 30 days; and either build the cross-site SSO or set SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN to the host-only app origin and mark docs/auth-integration.md as a rejected design. The last one is a 5-minute config change that shrinks the product session's exposure surface for free.
note: The storefront facts reproduce: src/lib/auth.js:20 says in terms 'Cons: cannot revoke a stolen session before 30-day expiry'; getSessionFromRequest (:293-303) does signature+exp only; _requireAdminSession (worker.js:6075-6085) compares the session email to env.NOTIFY_EMAIL, which is plaintext 'don@muntin.digital' in wrangler.jsonc vars. But the cross-repo direction is backwards. auth.js:24-27 sets the storefront cookie host-only with NO Domain, so the low-security half leaks nothing to the product. The exposure runs the other way — the PRODUCT's cookies carry Domain=muntin.digital (apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts:184-212, wrangler.toml SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN) and are therefore transmitted to the storefront Worker on every apex request. The report's recommendation (host-only the product cookie) happens to be right; its stated reason is not.

title: Self-serve GDPR erasure erases nothing, destroys the audit chain, and tells the customer the opposite
evidence: apps/api/src/routes/erasure.ts imports the audit, sessions, passkeys, document-deks, memberships, identity-key and users stores — and no documents or extractions store. The workspace route does exactly three durable things: record an audit event, `sessions.revokeAllForOrg` (:126), `tombstoneAuditChainForOrg` (:129). It never sets retention_until, never marks a row, never enqueues anything. The only automated deleter is scheduled/retention-reaper.ts, which is driven by each document's own retention_until (documents-store.ts:310-325, :630) and, when it fires, deletes the R2 object and calls markR2Purged — it issues no row DELETE anywhere. The only path that removes Neon rows is the MANUAL founder process in runbooks/account-deletion.md:37 ('Postgres documents rows (cascades to extractions...)'). Yet erasure.ts:153 returns to the customer: 'the stored invoice objects and database rows are scheduled for permanent deletion by the retention process within 24 hours.' The same response (:154) says 'Re-signing in will create a new workspace if you used the same email' — findOrCreateUser at routes/auth.ts:628-638 looks the address up and returns `{...existing, is_new: false}`, so the customer signs straight back into the SAME org with every document, extraction and vendor row intact.
impact: The product's Art. 17 surface is inverted: it permanently destroys the one artifact the company sells as its integrity guarantee (the audit chain — the rewrite is irreversible by design, audit.ts:296-300), preserves all the personal data, and issues a written 24-hour deletion assertion the system cannot honour. A customer who requests erasure and later checks — or a regulator who does — finds their invoices still present after the promised window, with the log that would have shown what happened overwritten. That is a materially worse story than 'we have not enabled the reaper yet,' because the honest reaper-off copy branch at erasure.ts:152 gives a false impression too (it says deletion is merely 'queued').
rec: Do not add an owner-only gate and call this closed. Either (a) make the route real — set retention_until = now on every document in the org so the reaper actually sweeps them, and add an org-scoped Neon purge for documents/extractions/vendors — or (b) make the copy true today: say plainly that access is revoked immediately, the audit chain is tombstoned, and permanent deletion of stored data is a manual operator step completed within N days via runbooks/account-deletion.md, with a contact address. Fix the false 'new workspace' sentence in the same edit. Then add the owner gate.

title: CORS trusts every *.muntin.digital origin with credentials, the session cookie spans the apex, and the CSRF token is JS-readable — so any storefront-side script owns the ledger
evidence: apps/api/src/index.ts:148-160 configures `cors({ credentials: true, origin: (origin, c) => { const appOrigin = c.env.APP_ORIGIN; if (origin === appOrigin) return origin; const root = appOrigin.replace(/^https?:\/\//,''); if (origin.endsWith(`.${root}`)) return origin; ... } })`. apps/api/wrangler.toml [vars] sets APP_ORIGIN = "https://muntin.digital" — the APEX, not the app host — so the credentialed allow-list is muntin.digital plus every subdomain, with no scheme check. In the same file SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN = "muntin.digital", and routes/auth.ts:184-212 issues muntin_session httpOnly/SameSite=Lax/Domain=muntin.digital, muntin_refresh httpOnly/Strict, and muntin_csrf with `httpOnly: false` on the same domain. middleware/csrf.ts:63-72 accepts any request whose x-csrf-token header equals that JS-readable cookie. Subdomains in play today: the 9,196-line storefront Worker on the apex, and status.muntin.digital, which infra/status-page/deploy.md:43 binds by `CNAME status -> muntin-status.pages.dev`.
impact: Script execution on ANY muntin.digital origin — a stored XSS in the storefront's Window/submissions surfaces, a compromised status page, a dangling-CNAME subdomain takeover, or a future preview deploy — reads muntin_csrf from document.cookie and issues fully authenticated, credentialed fetches to api.muntin.digital: export the ledger, delete documents, post bills to QuickBooks, or POST /v1/erasure. The product's carefully built session hygiene (15-minute tokens, jti revocation, kid pinning) is irrelevant against this because the attacker is inside the trust boundary the CORS policy grants. The blast radius of the LOWER-assurance half of the estate is therefore the whole product, which is precisely the inverse of the separation the two-repo architecture implies.
rec: Three config-level changes, no redesign: (1) point APP_ORIGIN at https://app.muntin.digital and drop the `endsWith('.'+root)` branch in favour of an explicit allow-list array — subdomain wildcards with credentials:true are never worth it for a two-origin product; (2) set SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN to the app host so the session and CSRF cookies stop being transmitted to the storefront Worker at all (docs/auth-integration.md's cross-site SSO was never built, so nothing depends on the wide scope); (3) if a same-site read of the CSRF cookie must stay possible, bind the token to the session jti rather than accepting bare equality. Add a gate asserting APP_ORIGIN !== the apex, since this is a one-line regression.

title: Two route files re-implement authentication and skip the revocation and key-rotation checks the rest of the API relies on
evidence: apps/api/src/routes/identity-key.ts:50-62 and apps/api/src/routes/passkey.ts:97-110 each define a private `resolveAuthedUser` that reads the muntin_session cookie, calls verifyJwt with audience/issuer, rejects only `token_use === "refresh"`, and returns {user_id, org_id}. Compare middleware/require-auth.ts:100-124, which additionally (a) requires token_use to be exactly 'access' when present, (b) pins `payload.kid` against env.JWT_KEY_KID, and (c) looks the jti up in the durable D1 sessions row and 401s when `revoked_at` is set. Neither custom resolver does any of the three. identity-key.ts is mounted at index.ts:167 and gates POST /remove (its own header, :34, states the user 'accepts that encrypted originals become unrecoverable') and POST /rotate; passkey.ts:208 gates credential registration. Note also that erasure's own defence — 'after this returns, requireAuth will 401 every caller bearing a previously-valid access token' (erasure.ts:37-41) — is false for these two files.
impact: Every revocation surface the company built has a hole in it. 'Sign out everywhere', the erasure session sweep, and an incident-response session kill all leave a stolen or revoked access token able to call POST /v1/auth/identity-key/remove for up to its 15-minute lifetime — destroying the key that decrypts every E2EE document the user owns — or to enrol a passkey that survives the incident as a persistent backdoor. A JWT_SECRET rotation, which the report correctly lists as a top strength, likewise does not invalidate in-flight tokens on these routes because kid is never compared. The two files chosen for bespoke auth are the two that manage credentials, which is the worst possible selection.
rec: Delete both `resolveAuthedUser` copies and mount `requireAuth` on the identity-key and passkey sub-apps; where passkey/register/begin needs a softer 401 body, wrap requireAuth rather than reimplement it. Then add the gate this codebase is good at: a script that fails CI on any route file importing `verifyJwt` directly instead of the middleware, with an allow-list for auth.ts and per-doc-jwt.ts. That gate would also have caught this at write time.

title: The warrant canary is 88 days stale, three cycles missed, and was never published at the URL it names — a document whose lapse it defines as the signal
evidence: docs/warrant-canary.md:3 'Last updated and signed: 2026-05-10'. :37-39 'This statement is updated on the first day of each calendar month. The next scheduled update is 2026-06-01.' :33 'If the warrant canary disappears or stops being updated on schedule, draw your own conclusions.' Against 2026-08-06 that is 88 days and three missed updates (Jun 1, Jul 1, Aug 1). :51-55 says the published version 'lives at muntin.digital/ledger/canary with a detached PGP signature' — no HTML file in the storefront repo contains the string 'canary', and there is no /ledger/canary/ directory; the signature and fingerprint remain literal bracketed placeholders (:47-49). The statement itself also asserts things the code does not support: item 5 covers loss of custody of any production credential, and the closing paragraph asserts 'All customer data is encrypted at rest' plus a BYOK tier described as Phase 4 (unbuilt).
impact: A warrant canary is the one security artifact whose failure mode is inverted: silence is the message. Either it stays current or it should not exist. Publishing it in-repo, three cycles stale, with the founder signature never attached, means the company has built an instrument that — read literally, by exactly the privacy-attentive buyer this product targets — currently signals a secret government order. Every competitor-comparison and trust-centre page that leans on privacy architecture is downstream of this. It is also the cheapest thing on the whole findings list to fix.
rec: Pick one of two, today. Retire it: delete docs/warrant-canary.md and record an ADR saying a one-person pre-revenue company will not commit to a monthly signing cadence it cannot keep, which is honest and defensible. Or ship it: re-sign with the real PGP key, publish at /ledger/canary on the storefront, and add a check-*.mjs gate that fails when the file's date is more than 35 days old — the storefront repo already runs exactly this pattern for check-cost-index-dispatch-fresh.mjs, so the machinery exists.

title: The storefront publishes security promises the product cannot keep, including a deletion claim and a third, conflicting disclosure SLA
evidence: ledger/index.html (storefront) ships the sentence 'Delete it and it's gone.' as a headline promise about the paid product — against the erasure route above, which deletes nothing and whose own reaper-off branch admits deletion is only 'queued'. security/index.html promises 'Security reports get the fastest reply turnaround on the site — within 24 hours, weekends included', while .well-known/security.txt in the same repo says 'Don will reply within 2 business days' and the product repo's docs/security.txt says 3 days — three published, mutually inconsistent response commitments against a founder working full-time front-of-house shifts. security.txt also still describes the company as 'a one-person studio', the retired services-line framing that check-positioning-drift.mjs exists to catch but does not scan .well-known.
impact: 'Delete it and it's gone' is the single most falsifiable sentence on the storefront and the one a journalist or competitor would test first: sign up, upload, request erasure, observe the data. It is a stronger deceptive-practices shape than the E2EE wording the report focused on, because it is unconditional, present-tense, and about a mechanism that is provably absent rather than merely opt-in. The conflicting SLAs are smaller but compound: a researcher who follows security.txt and waits 2 business days can point at the /security/ page's 24-hour promise as evidence the company does not honour its own published terms.
rec: Change the ledger page to what the system does — 'Export it whenever you want; ask us to delete it and we will' — until the erasure route actually deletes. Collapse the three SLAs to one number (2 business days is the only one a single employed person can hold) and make .well-known/security.txt the single source, with the /security/ page and the product doc quoting it. Extend check-positioning-drift.mjs's root list to .well-known and docs/ so the next drift is caught by the gate that already exists for this.

title: Diagnostic endpoints in both repos hand out cross-tenant counts and the full admin route inventory to callers who should not have them
evidence: apps/api/src/routes/db-diag.ts:44-52 — GET /v1/diag/db, gated by requireAuth only with the in-file rationale 'effectively the operator only', runs `set_config('app.org_id','diag')` then `select count(*)::int from documents`. Because documents is one of the 8 tables with no RLS (confirmed above), that count is the GLOBAL row count across every tenant, returned to any authenticated user, alongside DATABASE_URL length and up to 800 characters of raw Neon error text on failure. In the storefront, src/worker.js:2204-2233 handlePing is dispatched at :347 with no session check and returns `routes: Object.keys(API_ROUTES)` — the complete endpoint inventory including every /api/admin/* path — plus a `configured` map reporting which secrets and bindings are provisioned (resend, psi, places, AUDIT_CACHE, AI).
impact: Neither is a breach; both are free reconnaissance. /v1/diag/db is the first working demonstration that the documents RLS gap has real consequences — a customer can learn the size of the entire customer base, and the unredacted Neon error string is a credible path to leaking connection metadata. /api/ping tells an unauthenticated attacker exactly which admin endpoints to probe and which integrations are live, which is the enumeration step the storefront's single-email admin gate would otherwise cost them.
rec: Put /v1/diag/db behind requireFounder (which is already fail-closed at middleware/require-founder.ts:76 and mounted on /v1/ops) rather than requireAuth, and truncate or drop the raw error passthrough. In the storefront, drop `routes` from the ping payload entirely and gate the `configured` map behind _requireAdminSession, leaving ping as a bare liveness probe.

title: The published privacy policy states a deletion that the system cannot perform — and the code knows it
effort: 2 hours for the doc correction; 1 day including the live dry-run verification before arming
evidence: docs/privacy-policy.md:559 'the retention reaper removes the R2 objects + Postgres rows within 24 hours' and :591 'The 24-hour retention reaper deletes the R2 objects + cleartext Postgres rows you used to own after either deletion path.' Both are flat assertions. The reaper is double-locked OFF: STATUS-v6.md:1099-1100 'reaper double-locked (RETENTION_REAPER_DRYRUN=true set, RETENTION_REAPER_ENABLED absent) — cannot delete'; runbooks/r2-lifecycle.md:76-77 and runbooks/first-deploy.md:246 confirm the same posture; apps/api/src/scheduled/retention-reaper.ts gates every destructive step on `env.RETENTION_REAPER_DRYRUN === 'true'`. The same document hedges correctly in two other places (:164, :296 'the retention reaper, which is being enabled'), so it contradicts itself. apps/api/src/routes/erasure.ts:146-152 branches on the real flag and refuses to say '24 hours' — the runtime copy is honest while the published policy is not. The policy is served public + indexed at /legal/privacy (apps/web/app/(marketing)/legal/privacy/page.tsx:31 robots index:true) and is baked into the build (scripts/build-legal-content.mjs LEGAL_DOCS 'privacy:en').
impact: A privacy-positioned company has published, in the document a buyer reads to decide whether to trust it, a statement about the disposal of their invoice data that is false. This is the one claim the whole product is sold on. It is an FTC Act §5 deception exposure independent of any privacy statute, and docs/dpa.md §2's 30-day deletion commitment has no mechanism behind it. It also poisons the well retroactively: a customer who later learns the reaper was off will reasonably assume everything else was theatre too.
rec: Today: rewrite privacy-policy.md §'Your data deletion rights' (:552-597) and the ES mirror docs/es/privacy-policy.md to the exact wording erasure.ts:151 already uses ('permanent deletion ... is queued and will be completed when the retention process runs'), and remove the '24-hour retention reaper' as a stated mechanism until it is armed. Then, separately, arm it per runbooks/r2-lifecycle.md: set RETENTION_REAPER_DRYRUN=true, confirm `retention_reaper.tick` dry-run lines in `wrangler tail`, then set RETENTION_REAPER_ENABLED=true and delete the dryrun secret. Add a gate that parses the deployed flag posture and fails when the policy text and the flag disagree — the same shape as check-cost-index-snapshot-freshness.mjs.
note: Reproduced. docs/privacy-policy.md:559 and :591 assert the 24-hour reaper; :164 and :296 hedge ("being enabled"). apps/api/src/routes/erasure.ts:146-152 branches on RETENTION_REAPER_ENABLED and refuses the 24h wording. scripts/build-legal-content.mjs:59 bakes privacy:en/es, so both are served at /legal/privacy with robots index:true. Two corrections to the auditor: (a) the hedge at :164 is ALSO false — it says "explicit deletion (honored within 60s) is the guaranteed path", but erasure.ts:151's honest branch says permanent deletion is only *queued* until the retention process runs, so the fallback the policy offers does not exist either; (b) the company already self-discloses this exact gap on an INDEXED public surface — apps/web/lib/verify-content.generated.ts:391-413 (threat model §7, served at /verify, robots index:true) states that if the disabled_in_prod event fires "the privacy-policy 'deleted in 24h' claim is silently false". Published self-disclosure of a known gap with zero customers is not the same deception posture as concealment, so high, not critical. Severity is still high because the fix is a 20-minute doc edit that has sat undone since 2026-05-17.

title: The warrant canary is 88 days stale, unsigned, and was never published anywhere
effort: 2 hours to retire; 1 day to publish, sign, and gate
evidence: docs/warrant-canary.md 'Last updated and signed: 2026-05-10' (88 days ago) with 'Cadence: updated on the first day of each calendar month. The next scheduled update is 2026-06-01' — 2026-06-01, 2026-07-01 and 2026-08-01 have all been missed. The signature block still contains literal placeholders: 'Founder signature: [GPG signature attaches when the published version goes live]'. The document names its publication URL as muntin.digital/ledger/canary; /home/user/potentially-profitable/ledger/ contains only index.html and demo/, and `grep -ril canary --include=*.html` across the entire storefront returns nothing. scripts/build-legal-content.mjs's LEGAL_DOCS registry bakes privacy/terms/ropa/dpia and does NOT include the canary, so no /legal route serves it either. No check-*.mjs in either repo tests canary freshness (40 product gates, 129 storefront gates, zero).
impact: The document's own text is the trap: 'If the warrant canary disappears or stops being updated on schedule, draw your own conclusions' and 'take that as the strongest public signal we are legally able to give.' Three consecutive missed months is, by the company's own published rule, a signal that Muntin has been served with a secret order. The moment anyone reads this repo or a future published copy, the founder has manufactured a reputational crisis out of a scheduling lapse. The mitigating fact — that it was never actually published — is itself the finding: the trust artifact does not exist for customers, only for auditors reading the repo.
rec: Pick one and do it this week. (a) Retire it: delete docs/warrant-canary.md, remove the cross-references in transparency.md and transparency-2026q2.md, and state plainly on /verify that Muntin does not operate a warrant canary because a one-person company cannot guarantee the cadence. Or (b) run it properly: sign it with a real PGP key, publish at a real URL (add it to LEGAL_DOCS and a /legal/canary route), move the cadence to quarterly (achievable), and add a check-canary-freshness.mjs that fails CI at 100 days. Do not leave it as-is. An unsustainable canary is strictly worse than no canary.
note: The staleness math checks out (docs/warrant-canary.md:3 = 2026-05-10, 88 days) and `grep -ril canary --include=*.html` across the storefront returns nothing. But the auditor read past the doc's own §"Before publication (template fill-ins)" at :44-52: 'These placeholders are completed when this canary is published at muntin.digital/ledger/canary. They are intentionally left as literal brackets in the repo so they cannot be confused with a signed statement.' This is an explicitly-labelled pre-publication template, not a live trust artifact that lapsed — so the 'three missed months manufactures a reputational crisis' impact cannot fire on any reader who is not reading the repo, and 'unsigned' is a designed state, not a defect. The real finding is one the auditor buried: the PUBLISHED privacy policy asserts the canary exists (legal-content.generated.ts:143, :280 → served at /legal/privacy), while apps/web/lib/markdown.ts:120-127 deliberately drops warrant-canary.md links because there is no public route — the live policy claims an artifact and silently renders it unreachable. Medium, and the fix is one sentence in the policy, not a signing ceremony.

title: The published Art. 30 record denies a sub-processor the storefront demonstrably uses on every page
effort: 4 hours for the doc + config decision; 1 day including a cross-repo gate
evidence: docs/ropa.md:109 (activity A4, marketing-site analytics): 'Plausible-the-company is not a sub-processor — the software is self-hosted; no analytics data leaves our Fly instance.' docs/sub-processors.md:69 repeats it. The reality on muntin.digital: potentially-profitable/index.html:69-72 loads /assets/p.js with `plausible.init({ endpoint: '/api/event' })`; potentially-profitable/src/worker.js:8699 `const PLAUSIBLE_UPSTREAM = 'https://plausible.io/api/event'`; handlePlausibleEvent (:8700-8742) forwards the body to plausible.io with `'user-agent': userAgent` and `'x-forwarded-for': clientIp` taken from cf-connecting-ip. The tracker is on every page including privacy.html and cookies.html. The product app's own proxy (apps/web/app/api/event/route.ts) does point at a self-hosted CE — but its default is `http://plausible-ce.internal.invalid/api/event`, so ROPA A4 describes an arrangement that is unreachable in one repo and contradicted in the other. scripts/check-subprocessor-freshness.mjs cannot see this: it scans 94 IaC files inside Muntin-Invoice-Decoder only.
impact: Plausible Analytics OÜ receives the IP address and User-Agent of every visitor to muntin.digital and is named nowhere in the sub-processor register that docs/dpa.md §6 makes contractually binding. An undeclared sub-processor is a DPA breach the day the first customer signs. Worse for a company whose differentiation is verifiable honesty: the ROPA is published and indexed at /legal/ropa, so the falsifiable claim is the public one. The gate that exists to catch exactly this passed green because its root list omits the repo where the behaviour lives — the identical failure the storefront's own CLAUDE.md documents having learned three times.
rec: Decide which arrangement is true and make both repos and both documents say it. If muntin.digital keeps proxying to plausible.io, add Plausible Analytics OÜ (Estonia) as sub-processor row 12 with its region and DPA status, rewrite ROPA A4's recipients + international-transfers rows, and correct the Fly.io footnote in sub-processors.md:69. If the CE instance is the intent, point PLAUSIBLE_UPSTREAM at it and keep the current text. Then extend check-subprocessor-freshness.mjs's root list to the storefront (a checked-out sibling path or a mirrored gate in potentially-profitable/scripts/) and declare the omission in a comment if you cannot.
note: The code is exactly as described: src/worker.js:8699 PLAUSIBLE_UPSTREAM = 'https://plausible.io/api/event' and :8720-8733 forwards the body with user-agent and x-forwarded-for from cf-connecting-ip. But the auditor's framing — 'the ROPA denies a sub-processor the storefront demonstrably uses' — misreads scope. docs/sub-processors.md:58-65 (the A4 preamble) names the exact files it is describing: apps/web/public/assets/p.js, app/(marketing)/_components/PlausibleAnalytics.tsx, app/api/event/route.ts. ROPA A4 is a record of app.muntin.digital's marketing routes; it never purports to cover muntin.digital, a different Worker in a different repo. So this is a COVERAGE gap (no Art. 30 activity covers the storefront's analytics at all), not a denial of a known fact — which is the same defect as finding #9, not a separate high. Also worth noting against the auditor: the storefront's own privacy.html:452 DOES disclose Plausible as a vendor and correctly says 'your browser never makes a request directly to plausible.io' (true — the Worker does it server-side), so site visitors are not undisclosed-to. Medium.

title: The storefront privacy policy names four vendors; the Worker calls Google three ways and Anthropic once, and names a vendor that appears in no code
effort: 3 hours for the copy; 1 day with a gate
evidence: potentially-profitable/privacy.html:456 'Four third parties touch the data tied to this site' — Cloudflare, Resend, Plausible, Buttondown. The Worker calls: places.googleapis.com (src/worker.js:2258 searchText, :4315 place details), googleapis.com/pagespeedonline (:3815), chromeuxreport.googleapis.com (:4219), and `env.AI.run('@cf/anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5', ...)` gated on `env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (:4400, :4487) — the brand-dossier handler takes a user-submitted URL plus derived signals and sends them to Anthropic through Cloudflare AI Gateway. Meanwhile 'Buttondown' appears in exactly two files site-wide — privacy.html and es/privacy.html — and in zero code; the newsletter path (`/api/subscribe`, `subscriberConfirmEmail`, `handleCostIndexBroadcast`) runs on Resend. privacy.html:439 states 'Tools run in your browser; their inputs never reach a server' and scopes AI use to 'the studio (drafts, alt text, search cross-links)'. Last reviewed 2026-05-02 — 96 days ago.
impact: The vendor list is wrong in both directions: three real processors of user-submitted input are missing, and one listed processor may not exist. The 'inputs never reach a server' sentence is false for the audit/observatory tool family, which posts to the Worker and out to Google and Anthropic. This is the storefront's equivalent of the ROPA problem and is more visible — privacy.html is the page a skeptical operator reads first, and it is the page the /security/ 'nine claims, five tests' surface points at.
rec: Rewrite privacy.html §Vendors (and es/privacy.html) to list every third party the Worker actually contacts, with what each one receives: Cloudflare (hosting + Workers AI Gateway), Resend (email), Plausible (aggregate analytics, receives IP+UA), Google (Places / PageSpeed / CrUX — receives the URL or business name you type into an audit tool), Anthropic (receives the audit signals for the one-paragraph dossier). Delete Buttondown or confirm the list exists off-repo. Rewrite the 'inputs never reach a server' sentence to name which tools are client-only (Margin Math, Plate Cost, Menu Engineering) and which are server-backed. Add a storefront check-vendor-disclosure.mjs mirroring the product's freshness gate.
note: Reproduced the calls: src/worker.js:2258 + :4315 places.googleapis.com, :3815 pagespeedonline, :4219 chromeuxreport, :4487 env.AI.run('@cf/anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5') gated on env.AI && env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (:4400); wrangler.jsonc:345 binds "ai". Buttondown appears only in privacy.html and es/privacy.html and in zero code — confirmed. But 'Anthropic is missing' is partly refuted: privacy.html's AI sentence links to /ai/, and ai/index.html:457-459 discloses by name 'Claude (Anthropic)', 'GPT-class models (OpenAI)', 'Claude Code' and OpenAI embeddings with the training-opt-out posture. The genuinely false sentence is the narrower one — privacy.html:439 'Tools run in your browser; their inputs never reach a server' and 'The site has no server-side telemetry on any tool input' — which the audit/observatory tool family contradicts by posting a user-typed business name or URL to the Worker and out to Google. Google (three APIs) is the real undeclared processor. Medium, not high.

title: Cookie policy misses a 90-day tracking cookie; privacy policy claims a 90-day IP-hash purge that no code performs
effort: 1 day
evidence: cookies.html:450 'Three cookies. That's the entire list. There is no fourth.' But src/worker.js:6542 `const WINDOW_ANON_COOKIE_NAME = 'md_anon_thread_id'` with :6543 `MAX_AGE = 90 * 24 * 60 * 60`, set by _setWindowAnonCookie (:6569-6577) as a persistent per-device identifier for anonymous Window visitors. Separately, apps/api/wrangler.toml sets `SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN = 'muntin.digital'` (the apex), so muntin_session / muntin_refresh / the CSRF cookie issued by api.muntin.digital are also presented to the storefront — neither is listed. On retention: privacy.html:432 'the IP hash is dropped at 90 days.' src/worker.js:6256 writes the submission row with `put(submissionKey(auth.sub, id), JSON.stringify(row))` — no expirationTtl; the only TTL in the path is REJECTED_TTL_SEC on rejections (:6331). No 90-day drop exists anywhere in src/. And the hash salt is `env.MAGIC_LINK_BASE_URL || 'muntin'` (:6241) — a public constant — so a SHA-256 over the 2^32 IPv4 space is trivially reversible; 'one-way' overstates it.
impact: Two false statements in two published policies, one of them a cookie disclosure (the exact artifact regulators and ePrivacy read literally) and one a retention promise. The IP hashes of every field-note submitter are retained indefinitely and are de-anonymisable by anyone who reads privacy.html to learn the salt. For a site whose /never/ and /security/ pages are built on 'inspect this yourself', a reader who opens DevTools and finds a fourth cookie has disproved the page in ten seconds.
rec: Add md_anon_thread_id to cookies.html and es/cookies.html with purpose, 90-day lifespan and the strictly-necessary argument; add a line noting that signing into Muntin Ledger sets apex-domain session cookies visible here. Either add `{ expirationTtl: 90*24*3600 }` on the ipHash field (better: strip the ipHash from the row on approval and keep it only in a short-TTL throttle key) or delete the 90-day claim from privacy.html:432. Replace the constant salt with a rotating secret. Add a storefront gate that greps Set-Cookie names in src/ and fails when one is absent from cookies.html — the shape sentinel is cheap and would have caught this.
note: Fully reproduced and, if anything, understated. src/worker.js:6542-6543 defines md_anon_thread_id at 90 days; :6571-6577 sets it; :6915 calls _setWindowAnonCookie inside handleWindowAppend — a live route, not dead code — and wrangler.jsonc:226 WINDOW_ENABLED="true" plus :235 WINDOW_ANON_ENABLED="true" are committed, so the fourth cookie ships today against cookies.html:450 'Three cookies. That's the entire list. There is no fourth.' apps/api/wrangler.toml:75 SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN="muntin.digital" (apex) confirms the product's session cookies are also presented on the storefront. On retention, src/lib/submissions.js's own header comment on the submission row reads 'idempotency key + audit trail; persists forever', and src/worker.js:6256 writes it with no expirationTtl — the code documents the opposite of privacy.html:432. One correction: the live salt is env.MAGIC_LINK_BASE_URL, which wrangler.jsonc:202 sets to 'https://muntin.digital'; the bare 'muntin' the auditor quoted is only the fallback. Still a public constant, so the reversibility point stands.

title: Self-serve account deletion leaves behind the data the privacy policy names by name
effort: 4 hours
evidence: privacy.html:423 'You can delete everything tied to your account at /account/; deletion takes effect within minutes' and :450 the same for Workshop accounts. privacy.html:430 defines what is tied to the account: 'Saved items, watches, and storefront-health properties live in a Cloudflare KV namespace tied to your account.' The cascade at src/worker.js:5578-5582 wipes exactly three things: `wipePrefix('save:' + sub + ':')`, `wipePrefix('watch:' + sub + ':')`, and `delete('user:' + sub)`. It does not touch `property:<sub>:` (src/lib/workbench.js:501 PROPERTY_KEY_PREFIX), `submission:<sub>:` (src/lib/submissions.js:33 — the rows carrying the ipHash), or `window:thread:<sub>:` (src/lib/window.js:38). No reaper or TTL exists for any of them, so the orphans are permanent. The two-step flow itself (typed-email match, 15-min single-use token, POST-only wipe) is well built — the defect is scope, not design.
impact: A user who exercises the deletion right and reads the confirmation ('Your account and every saved item have been deleted') keeps an undeleted record of their business domain, their site-health audit history, their field notes and their reversible IP hash in KV forever. Under any state deletion right and under the plain meaning of the published sentence, this is a failed erasure — and it is failed silently, with a success page.
rec: Add `wipePrefix('property:' + sub + ':')` and `wipePrefix('submission:' + sub + ':')` to the cascade at src/worker.js:5578; decide explicitly whether Window threads go too (privacy.html:429 currently carves them out as a manual path — if that stays, say so on the /account/ confirmation screen rather than 'every saved item'). Write a one-page test that seeds one key of every prefix, runs the cascade, and asserts zero remain — and wire it. Then re-word the success copy to enumerate what was removed.
note: Reproduced verbatim at src/worker.js:5578-5582: wipePrefix('save:'+sub+':'), wipePrefix('watch:'+sub+':'), delete('user:'+sub) — nothing else. property:, submission: and window:thread: survive, and privacy.html:430 names 'storefront-health properties' as data tied to the account while the success copy at :5588 says 'Your account and every saved item have been deleted.' No TTL exists on any of the three orphan prefixes. The two-step token flow is as well built as the auditor says; the defect is scope only.

title: The quarterly transparency report is 36 days past its own promised date and renders empty in production
effort: 1 day
evidence: docs/transparency-2026q2.md header: 'Partial — final report at 2026-07-01', covering 2026-04-01 to 2026-05-11. Today is 2026-08-06: the final is 36 days overdue and the partial's window closed 87 days ago. Worse, neither transparency page can render in production. apps/web/app/(marketing)/legal/transparency/page.tsx:28 `const DOCS_DIR = path.join(process.cwd(), '..', '..', 'docs')` with `readdir` at :52 inside a try/catch returning `[]`; the [quarter] page does the same at :25 and falls back to a 'not here yet' panel. scripts/build-legal-content.mjs:9-16 documents that this exact pattern fails in the deployed Cloudflare Worker ('the docs/ directory is not in the worker bundle. Caught in production 2026-05-27') and its own docstring says it bakes 'transparency reports' — but LEGAL_DOCS (:58-65) contains only privacy:en/es, terms:en/es, ropa:en, dpia:en. No transparency entry. So the index silently lists nothing.
impact: The company built a quarterly transparency cron (apps/api/src/scheduled/quarterly-transparency.ts, wired at wrangler.toml crons '0 6 1 1,4,7,10 *'), an aggregator, a public index route and a first report — and the public surface shows an empty list because of a bug whose fix was already written for the neighbouring pages. Every cross-reference in privacy-policy.md, ropa.md and warrant-canary.md points readers at a page that has nothing on it. The overdue Q2 final compounds it: the report promises its own replacement date and missed it.
rec: Add `{ key: 'transparency:2026q2', path: 'docs/transparency-2026q2.md' }` (and a glob for future quarters) to LEGAL_DOCS in scripts/build-legal-content.mjs, and rewrite both transparency pages to read LEGAL_CONTENT instead of the filesystem — the privacy page is the working template. Then write the Q2 final: with zero customers every number is still zero, so it is a 20-minute edit, and publishing a zeroed final on time is a stronger trust signal than an elaborate partial that never resolves. Add a freshness gate that fails when a quarter has closed and no matching transparency-*.md exists.
note: Reproduced. docs/transparency-2026q2.md:3 'Partial — final report at 2026-07-01' (36 days overdue); apps/web/app/(marketing)/legal/transparency/page.tsx:28 DOCS_DIR = process.cwd()/../../docs with readdir in a try/catch; scripts/build-legal-content.mjs:9-16 documents that this exact pattern was caught failing in production 2026-05-27 and its LEGAL_DOCS at :58-65 has no transparency entry. Downgraded to medium: every number in a zero-customer transparency report is zero, no cross-referenced reader is a customer, and the fix is one array entry plus a page rewrite against a working template that already exists in the same directory.

title: Sub-processor register and deployed integration flags disagree in both directions, including on Square's 30-day notice
effort: 3 hours
evidence: docs/sub-processors.md:77 row 11: Square is '_planned, opt-in, not yet processing customer data_' with Since = 'Planned — 30-day notice required before enabling'. apps/api/wrangler.toml sets `INTEGRATIONS_SQUARE_ENABLED = 'true'` with a sandbox client id and `INTEGRATIONS_SQUARE_SANDBOX = 'true'`. Rows 7 and 8 (Intuit, Xero) say 'Both true as of 2026-05-25' and Since = '2026-05-25 (activated; DPA pending signature)'; the same wrangler.toml sets `INTEGRATIONS_QBO_ENABLED = 'false'` and `INTEGRATIONS_XERO_ENABLED = 'false'` with a comment 'Pre-launch (replan §A/E): integrations are deferred'. The freshness gate (scripts/check-subprocessor-freshness.mjs) passes because it checks vendor-token presence and row age, not flag state.
impact: docs/dpa.md §6 makes the sub-processor list the contractual notice mechanism with a 30-day clock. Today the register says a vendor is not enabled while the deploy config enables it, and says two vendors are activated while the deploy config disables them. Neither error has a customer today, but the register is precisely the artifact that must be right on day one of the first paid contract — and the sandbox flag means the 30-day clock for Square was never started against a real customer set.
rec: Reconcile the three rows against wrangler.toml today and record the reconciliation date. Then extend check-subprocessor-freshness.mjs with a flag-state assertion: parse INTEGRATIONS_*_ENABLED out of apps/api/wrangler.toml and fail when a row's stated status contradicts the flag. That is a ~30-line addition to a gate that already reads the IaC, and it converts a documentation-hygiene problem into a mechanical one.
note: Reproduced: apps/api/wrangler.toml:139 INTEGRATIONS_SQUARE_ENABLED="true" against docs/sub-processors.md:77 row 11 'Planned — 30-day notice required before enabling'; :124-125 QBO/Xero = "false" against rows 7-8 '2026-05-25 (activated)'. The gate passes for exactly the reason given (I ran it: 'OK — 94 IaC files, 14 vendors named, 6 active rows'). The auditor under-called the blast radius: the drift is not confined to markdown. apps/api/src/routes/posture.ts:26-30 and routes/data-map.ts:109-139 each hardcode a SIX-vendor array that is served to customers as the privacy posture sheet and the /settings/data-map surface, with a comment that they mirror the markdown 'so the UI does not have to fetch the markdown'. That is three copies of the sub-processor register with a gate over only one of them. Medium is right for today (no customers), but the recommendation should include the two TS arrays.

title: The ROPA declares four processing activities; the code runs at least nine
effort: 2 days for the ROPA additions; 1 day for the route-coverage gate
evidence: docs/ropa.md:17-20 scopes itself to A1 account management, A2 invoice extraction, A3 QBO/Xero integrations, A4 marketing analytics. Last updated 2026-05-29 (69 days).
