More usefully it is a marker of an abandoned design pass shipped to 378 pages, and the kind of dead markup that makes a future 'why does the homepage look flat' investigation take an hour longer than it should.
rec: Decide once: either write the intended treatment (the name suggests a distinct below-the-fold surface tier, which the section-rhythm system in check-contrast.mjs already has tokens for) or strip the class from all 378 pages in a single injector pass. Do not leave it. If a rule is written, add its text/surface pair to check-contrast.mjs's T table so the new tier is covered from day one.

title: Bus factor is exactly 1 with no succession, no credential inventory, and an unrecoverable key — both repos sit on one personal GitHub account
effort: 1 day for (1)+(2); (3) is a half-day of AWS config plus a decision
evidence: `git remote -v` in both trees resolves to `github.com/Donwonmagic/potentially-profitable` and `github.com/Donwonmagic/Muntin-Invoice-Decoder` — a personal account, not an organization. `Muntin-Invoice-Decoder/.github/CODEOWNERS` is the single line `* @donwonmagic`; the storefront has no CODEOWNERS at all (`ls -a .github/` returns only `workflows`). A grep across both repos for `bus factor|succession|next of kin|estate|continuity plan|dead man` returns zero matches in any doc — the only hits are React `useState` and unrelated prose. Meanwhile the credential surface is large and entirely undocumented as an inventory: `apps/api/wrangler.toml` + env types name `JWT_SECRET`, `CHAIN_HEAD_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY`, `RESEND_API_KEY`, `APNS_PRIVATE_KEY_P8_BASE64`, `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY_P8_BASE64`, `SQUARE_CLIENT_SECRET`, `SENTRY_DSN`; `runbooks/first-deploy.md` adds Cloudflare, Neon, Fly, AWS KMS and a billing card for each; `docs/sub-processors.md:67-77` lists 11 vendor relationships (6 active, 5 planned); the storefront adds FRED/BLS/AMS/LMR/EIA repo secrets plus the ADR-013 NASS/Census/EIA keys that CLAUDE.md says live only on the operator's Mac; `runbooks/desktop-release-publish.md:30` puts the Tauri signing private key in 'the engineer's password manager'; `runbooks/two-person-prod-approval.md:60-63` depends on a `muntin-founder` PGP key. And `runbooks/backup-restore-drill.md:65-67`: 'KMS keys are NOT in backup; if the KMS key is lost, ciphertext is unrecoverable.'
impact: One event — death, incapacity, a lost 2FA device, a GitHub account lockout — permanently ends the company and, once customers exist, permanently destroys their encrypted invoice archive. GitHub offers no recovery path for an incapacitated personal-account owner short of a legal process; AWS KMS offers none at all for a lost CMK. There is no second human who could restore a database, rotate a secret, update an expiring card, or answer security@. Every other finding in this audit is downstream of this one.
rec: Three things this month, in order. (1) Write `docs/continuity.md`: a plain-text inventory of every account, who the registrar/vendor is, what breaks if it lapses, and a named human (spouse, sibling, attorney) with sealed recovery instructions — do NOT put secrets in it, put the location of the vault and the recovery process. (2) Move both repos into a GitHub organization and add one trusted second owner; this is free, takes 20 minutes, and simultaneously un-blocks the two-person deploy control that is currently impossible (see `two-person-approval-impossible`). (3) Get the AWS KMS CMK under a documented recovery path before a single customer's invoice is encrypted with it — today there are no customers, so this is the cheapest it will ever be.
note: Reproduced every artifact. `git remote -v` in both trees → github.com/Donwonmagic/{potentially-profitable,Muntin-Invoice-Decoder}; Muntin-Invoice-Decoder/.github/CODEOWNERS is exactly `* @donwonmagic`; storefront `.github/` contains only `workflows`. `grep -rin "bus factor|succession|next of kin|continuity plan" --include=*.md` returns zero in both repos. runbooks/backup-restore-drill.md:65-67 reads verbatim as quoted. Severity stands. One thing they got wrong by omission and it matters: the two repos have DIFFERENT visibility — the GitHub API reports `private:false` for potentially-profitable and `private:true` for Muntin-Invoice-Decoder. The auditor treated them as one undifferentiated 'personal account' exposure and missed that half the company's internal record is already world-readable (see missed #3).

title: ~35 founder-hours/month of pure maintenance against a part-time capacity that is about to shrink — and the decay it predicts is already measurable
effort: 3–4 days of automation work to recover ~15 h/month, then ongoing
evidence: Built from the repos' own registries, not estimated in the abstract. Monthly Cost Index dispatch, hand-written and fact-gated: `blog/cost-index-week-2026-07-06/index.html` is 3,166 words with 4 figures and 3 `<details class="cite">` drawers (the 06-18 edition is 3,548 words) — call it 6.5h. Warrant canary re-sign, monthly (`docs/warrant-canary.md:36-39`) 0.5h. Cross-repo snapshot re-vendor ×2 on 30d/21d clocks (`apps/api/scripts/vendor-cost-index.mjs`, `vendor-cost-pressure.mjs`) ~1h. ADR-013 operator-Mac open-data fetch + 8 `(idem)` rebuilds — the `OPERATOR_DATA` block in `scripts/check-idem-coverage.mjs:62-77` — 1.5–6h; the six `data/*.jsonl` sources were last fetched 2026-07-24 (13 days ago) and `nass-crop-condition.jsonl` tracks a weekly source. Thirteen content-linked manual injectors (`check-idem-coverage.mjs:78-150`, `inject-knit-rail.mjs` flagged 'highest-churn') ~1.5h. Frozen-feed triage ~4h. Weekly `pnpm ship-friday` + the multi-target deploy sequence (`runbooks/this-evening.md` budgets '~20-30 minutes' per pass across 4 deploy targets) ~3h. CI-red triage across two repos ~4h. Reading 3 nightly product workflows + 2 storefront alarm workflows ~2h. Quarterly transparency report ~1h/mo amortized. Seven quarterly drills, each 2–4h, ~6h/mo amortized. 90-day secret rotations ~0.33h/mo. `security-operator-followups.md` after each security batch ~1h. Monthly competitor-claims drift issue ~0.5h. **Total ≈ 35 h/month ≈ 8 h/week, none of it revenue-producing.** Against capacity: Don is a full-time FOH manager at a two-location brand (evening- and weekend-heavy). The commit histogram is the honest evidence of when the side venture actually happens — 197 of 582 product commits (34%) and 87 of 343 storefront commits (25%) land between 00:00 and 05:00 local time. `docs/handoff/strategic-council-board.md` records the directive shift: 'the operator is starting a college course, with little time or money for a launch.' The predicted decay is already on the board: unexpected frozen feeds went 8 → 16 in seven days (board entry dated 2026-07-30 vs `check-cost-index-series-freshness` today); product-repo commits stopped 2026-07-31; storefront has 3 commits in August.
impact: Maintenance consumes 40–50% of discretionary capacity today and 80–160% of it once coursework starts. When capacity drops below maintenance, surfaces go dark in the order of their decay clocks — which is precisely the observed pattern. Because this is a company whose entire differentiation is that its published numbers are true, the failure mode is not a slow product: it is public claims quietly becoming false while ~160 CI gates stay green. That is the exact failure the 2026-07-30 audit already caught once.
rec: Treat the maintenance budget as a hard constraint and cut it to under 15 h/month before the course starts. Concretely: automate the four highest-ratio chores (see `automation-debt`), and then DELETE rather than maintain — the 8 ADR-013 open-data builders, the 13 content-linked injectors, and the seafood surfaces behind 10 known-latent feeds are each a candidate for retirement under the ADR-021 terminal-page path that already exists. Write the remaining obligations into one `docs/operating-calendar.md` with a monthly checklist so 'what is due' is a 60-second read, not a re-derivation across 71 runbooks and two registries.
note: The ~35 h/month inventory is a defensible floor built from real registries and I do not dispute it. Both empirical props under it are wrong. (a) 'frozen feeds went 8 → 16 in seven days' is a GATE IMPROVEMENT, not decay. I checked out 1f4f6475b (2026-07-30) into a worktree and ran its own gate against TODAY's clock: 8 unexpected, 82 fresh. Today's tree: 16 unexpected, 74 fresh. The delta is commit bc7b99285 (2026-07-31), which added `effectiveAsOf()` to check-cost-index-series-freshness.mjs:79-102 so the countdown uses the oldest level-provenance date, not the composite asOf. All 8 new rows carry `[STALE LEVEL ANCHOR]` — precisely the class the old gate could not see. Nothing decayed; the detector got better, which is the opposite of the auditor's headline. (b) '34% of product commits and 25% of storefront commits land 00:00–05:00 local time' is computed in the container's UTC. In America/New_York (Silver Spring): product 43/582 = 7.4%, storefront 31/343 = 9.0% — a 3–4× overstatement. Worse, 489 of 582 product commits and 274 of 343 storefront commits are authored by `Claude`, plus `muntin-cost-index-bot` and `Cursor Agent`; commit timestamps measure when an agent session or cron wrote, not founder hours. The histogram is not evidence of anything about Don's schedule.

title: The supply-pressure resolver goes dark on 2026-08-10; its gate is already failing and the only fix requires both repos on the founder's laptop
effort: 15 minutes to fix; 1 day to make permanent
evidence: `node Muntin-Invoice-Decoder/scripts/check-cost-pressure-snapshot-fresh.mjs` exits **1** today: 'STALE SOON — asOf 2026-07-20 is 17d old and the resolver stops answering past 21d.' The snapshot itself (`apps/api/src/data/cost-pressure-snapshot.json`) carries `asOf: "2026-07-20"`. The gate is wired into `.github/workflows/ci.yml:208-209`, so the product repo's node-lints job is red right now and any push or PR is blocked. The weekly alarm `cost-index-snapshot-watch.yml:48` fires Mondays 15:00 UTC with a 7-day lead — meaning it already fired on 2026-08-03 and has gone unactioned for three days. The sibling `cost-index-snapshot.json` reads `_asOfRange: "2026-07-18..2026-07-28"` and is fine today (9d of a 30d window) but crosses its own cliff on 2026-08-27. impact: In 4 days the Plate supply-pressure direction band silently returns nothing, exactly as the ADR-009 §7 lapse did for 42 days earlier this summer. It does not error, it does not log a customer-visible failure — it just stops answering, which is the failure class this company has already been bitten by once. Meanwhile the red gate blocks all product-repo CI, so even an unrelated one-line fix cannot merge.
rec: Run `node apps/api/scripts/vendor-cost-pressure.mjs && node apps/api/scripts/vendor-cost-index.mjs` with both repos checked out, commit both snapshots, today. Then do the automation in `automation-debt` so this is the last time it is a manual chore.
note: Reproduced: `node scripts/check-cost-pressure-snapshot-fresh.mjs` exits 1 with 'asOf 2026-07-20 is 17d old'; apps/api/src/data/cost-pressure-snapshot.json carries asOf 2026-07-20; ci.yml:206-209 wires it into node-lints. Two corrections. The remediation is available and would work: the storefront's data/pressure-observations.json is at asOf 2026-08-03 with _status 'live', so a re-vendor lands a fresh snapshot today. And 'the fix is literally impossible without both working trees side by side on one machine' is REFUTED — both scripts take the source path as argv (vendor-cost-index.mjs:33, vendor-cost-pressure.mjs:37-43) AND the storefront repo is public, so a workflow in the private product repo can `actions/checkout` it with the default GITHUB_TOKEN and no credential at all.

title: 22 documented alert rules, zero configured; the only channel that reaches the founder is a once-daily email — against a published 15-minute P1 SLA and a 99.5% uptime SLO
effort: 2 hours for the one monitor; half a day to honestly re-header the runbook
evidence: `runbooks/betterstack-alerts.md` specifies 22 rules (8 critical, 10 high, 3 medium, 1 info), each with a filter expression, page threshold and triage steps. Its routing (lines 31-34) sends `critical → PagerDuty (24/7 rotation)` and `high → PagerDuty (business-hours rotation) AND Slack #muntin-ops`. There is no PagerDuty account, no rotation, and no Slack workspace referenced anywhere in `infra/` or any workflow. Every rule depends on a log drain that does not exist: `runbooks/founder-todos.md` F14 is still open — '`funnel.*` events reaching log-drain … Provision the BetterStack (or similar) drain destination.' `runbooks/incident-response.md:22-26` is candid: 'Sprint 0: founder is sole on-call … Pager: BetterStack. Backup channel: SMS to founder's mobile. Both are set up in BetterStack on first day of paid beta' — i.e. neither exists yet. The only real channel is `apps/api/src/scheduled/ops-digest.ts`, a single daily email on the `0 12 * * *` cron that no-ops entirely when `FOUNDER_EMAIL` is unset (lines 44-58, `reason: "no_recipient"`). Against this: `incident-response.md:15` sets a 15-minute P1 first-response SLA, and `slos.md:57-58` publishes '99.5% monthly uptime … Roughly 3 hours 49 minutes of allowed downtime per month.'
impact: Realistic detection latency for a P1 is up to 24 hours (next digest), and remediation waits for the post-shift window the commit histogram shows is 00:00–05:00. Honest MTTR: 12–30 hours. A single undetected overnight incident burns 3–8× the entire published monthly error budget. Today there are no customers so the harm is reputational-only; on day one of paid beta the 15-minute SLA and the 99.5% SLO become claims the operating setup cannot possibly keep, which is a contractual and marketing-truth problem for a company selling honesty.
rec: Do not wire 22 rules. Wire ONE, this week: a single uptime monitor on `api.muntin.digital/health` that SMSes his phone, on the BetterStack free tier (10 monitors, $0 — `runbooks/first-deploy.md` already budgets it). Then either mark `betterstack-alerts.md` as 'designed, not configured' at the top of the file, or delete the PagerDuty/Slack routing that names infrastructure the company does not have. A runbook that describes a control nobody built is the 'appearance of protection' the product repo's own gate-coverage doctrine warns about.
note: Facts reproduced: runbooks/betterstack-alerts.md:31-34 routes to PagerDuty/Slack; grep finds no PagerDuty or Slack workspace in infra/ or any workflow; founder-todos.md:54 (F14) leaves the log drain unprovisioned; apps/api/src/scheduled/ops-digest.ts:44-58 returns `reason:"no_recipient"` when FOUNDER_EMAIL is unset. But the auditor's own citation undercuts the severity: incident-response.md:22-26 states 'Both are set up in BetterStack on first day of paid beta' — a written, dated deferral tied to an event that has not happened. With zero customers and launch deferred to 2027 (ADR-020), 'no on-call' is a documented tradeoff, not an unnoticed gap. The genuine finding is narrower and the auditor buried it: slos.md:57-58 publishes 99.5% uptime and incident-response.md:15 a 15-minute P1 SLA that the setup cannot keep. That is a copy-vs-capability problem worth a medium, not a high.

title: The two-person production-deploy control is architecturally unachievable — there is no GitHub org, and CODEOWNERS is the deployer himself
effort: 2 hours to re-document honestly; half a day to actually stand up an org + second owner
evidence: `.github/workflows/deploy.yml:20-31` documents the control: 'Required reviewers: 1 · Reviewer pool: any `@muntin` org member with the `deploy` role · "Prevent self-review": ON (so the deployer cannot approve their own deploy; this is what makes it two-person)' and asserts 'the repo CODEOWNERS includes this file so a PR that strips the gate cannot land without security-team review.' `runbooks/two-person-prod-approval.md:44-52` names the pool as `@founder`, `@on-call-primary`, `@on-call-secondary`, managed at `https://github.com/orgs/muntin/teams/deploy/members`. But `git remote -v` shows the repo is `github.com/Donwonmagic/Muntin-Invoice-Decoder` — a personal account. There is no `muntin` organization; personal-account repos have no teams. `.github/CODEOWNERS` is `* @donwonmagic`, so the 'security-team review' that supposedly protects the gate is Don reviewing Don. The runbook's own header (line 9) reads 'Last config check: Not yet executed (configure on first deploy)'.
impact: A control the company documents in three places, cites in its security posture, and built an off-hours PGP-signed override procedure for cannot be enabled at all. Either the `environment: production` job blocks forever with an unsatisfiable reviewer, or Don approves his own deploy and the gate is what the runbook itself calls 'theatre' (line 33). If this control is ever cited to a customer, an auditor, or a design partner as a shipped safeguard, that is a false claim about security posture.
rec: Move both repos into a GitHub organization (free) — this fixes the bus factor and this finding with one action. Until a genuine second principal exists, edit `deploy.yml`'s header and `two-person-prod-approval.md` to say the control is DESIGNED AND NOT CONFIGURED, with the date, exactly the way `check-gate-coverage.mjs`'s UNWIRED registry handles an unwired gate. Do not leave a security control documented as live when it is impossible.
note: Reproduced deploy.yml:20-31 and two-person-prod-approval.md:9 verbatim, and the repo is personal so `github.com/orgs/muntin/teams/deploy` cannot exist. But the auditor read the header comment and stopped at line 31. deploy.yml:65-100 is the real story: every one of the four deploy steps is `echo "TODO(B-priv-6): wire ... after cosign signing pipeline lands"`, and the 'Record deploy in audit log' step at 97-100 is also a TODO echo. The gate is not merely unconfigurable — it guards a workflow that deploys nothing and audits nothing. Promoting this to a separate missed finding (#2) because the auditor's evidence stops one screen short of it.

title: Nine mandatory drills have never been executed once — including the backup restore, whose procedure requires a second person who does not exist
effort: 1 full day for the backup drill; 2 hours to honestly re-cadence the rest
evidence: Every drill/rotation header table in `runbooks/` reads 'Not yet executed': `backup-restore-drill.md:9`, `incident-response.md:9`, `key-rotation.md:8`, `r2-lifecycle.md:9`, `account-deletion.md:9` (GDPR Art. 17), `data-export-art-20.md:8` (GDPR Art. 20), `extraction-degradation.md:10`, `byok-revocation.md:9`, `two-person-prod-approval.md:9`. `first-deploy.md:10` also reads 'Not yet executed' despite `this-evening.md` describing a live production Fly app with a kill-switch — the tables are simply never updated, so 'Not yet executed' is unreliable in both directions. Three specifics matter most. The backup drill's production path, step 2 (`backup-restore-drill.md:54-55`): 'Confirm the restore target … with at least one other person before proceeding' — there is no other person. Its stated targets are RTO 4h / RPO 1h, entirely unvalidated. And `key-rotation.md` mandates a 90-day `JWT_SECRET` rotation and a 90-day Cloudflare API token rotation, neither ever performed, while the KMS re-wrap helper it depends on does not exist ('`scripts/rewrap-deks.sh` lands MVP weeks 7-10; until then, run the equivalent against KMS by hand').
impact: The company's data-durability promise, its GDPR Art. 17/20 obligations, and its key-custody posture are all unproven. RTO/RPO numbers published to customers are aspirations, not measurements. A first real restore attempt would be a first attempt, under pressure, alone, on a restaurant floor. Pre-revenue this is cheap to fix; post-first-customer it is a regulatory and existential exposure.
rec: Run exactly ONE drill before any customer exists: the backup restore, end to end, on staging, timed, and write the elapsed time into the table at the top of the file. That single run either validates the 4h RTO or produces the most valuable finding in this company's ops history. Then delete or defer the other eight drill schedules explicitly — a quarterly cadence nobody can meet trains the founder to ignore the header. Rewrite the 'confirm with at least one other person' step to something a solo operator can actually perform (e.g. a 10-minute cool-off + a written pre-commitment of the restore timestamp).
note: All ten 'Not yet executed' headers reproduced at the cited lines. The framing 'nine mandatory drills' is inflated: byok-revocation.md:9 reads 'Not yet executed (BYOK is Phase 4)' with cadence 'Quarterly once BYOK ships'; backup-restore-drill.md:9 and incident-response.md:9 both read 'First Friday after MVP private beta'; two-person-prod-approval.md:9 reads 'configure on first deploy'; account-deletion and data-export-art-20 are GDPR obligations with no data subjects yet. By their own written triggers those are pre-cadence, not overdue. Exactly two are due unconditionally and unmet: key-rotation.md:8 and r2-lifecycle.md:9, both 'First Friday of each calendar quarter' with no event gate. The one genuinely damning detail the auditor found and buried — backup-restore-drill.md:54-55 requires confirming the restore target 'with at least one other person' and there is no other person — deserves to be the whole finding.

title: The gate built specifically to catch frozen data feeds is warn-only and is missing from the one alarm that runs during an absence — the roster doubled from 8 to 16 in seven days with nobody notified
effort: 1 hour for the wiring; 1 day for the 16 per-feed sourcing decisions
evidence: `node scripts/check-cost-index-series-freshness.mjs` today reports 16 unexpected frozen feeds plus 10 known-latent — 26 of 100 series ≥45 days stale — and **exits 0** (`--strict` exits 1). Two of the 16 are basket contributors (shrimp and vegetable-oil, both last read 2026-06-01, 67d), which is why `data/cost-index.json` carries `basket.asOf = 2026-06-01` (66 days old) alongside `_lastReviewed = 2026-08-05`. Eight of the 16 are flagged 'STALE LEVEL ANCHOR — composite reads 2026-08-04, but the price behind it is from 2026-05-11'. The gate is invoked in exactly one place, `.github/workflows/cost-index-refresh.yml:225`, deliberately warn-only ('a dead upstream must not block a refresh that is otherwise carrying good data forward') — so it prints into the log of a green run three times a week. Crucially it is **not** in `freshness-heartbeat.yml`, whose Saturday gate list (lines 67-73) covers seven other time-decay gates and was written 2026-07-28 — two days before this gate existed. Neither is `check-cost-index-orphans.mjs`. So the storefront's absence alarm is blind to the exact decay it was built for. Comparing today's roster to the board entry dated 2026-07-30 (which recorded 8 unexpected), the count doubled in one week. The earliest 120-day cliff is yellow-squash in 33 days (~2026-09-08), at which point the builder starts dropping ingredients.
impact: The public Cost Index — the company's entire top of funnel and, per the board's own strategy note, 'the company for the next year' — is publishing a basket whose anchor date is 66 days old while the page reads as freshly reviewed. Within 33 days ingredient pages begin retiring. The failure mode is the 2026-07-30 lesson repeating verbatim: a gate that measures the presence of a shape, running green, while the system underneath is not grounded in what it claims.
rec: Add `check-cost-index-series-freshness` and `check-cost-index-orphans` to the `GATES` list in `freshness-heartbeat.yml:67-73` this week — one line each, and the workflow already opens a rolling issue and fails the job. Separately, make the WARN visible where it matters: have the refresh workflow fail the job (not the commit) when the unexpected count *increases*, so growth is the signal, not absolute staleness. Then make the per-feed call the board's open item 1 demands: re-source or move into `KNOWN_SOURCE_LATENT` with a dated comment, starting with shrimp and vegetable-oil because they date the published headline.
note: The wiring gap is CONFIRMED and worth fixing: check-cost-index-series-freshness is invoked only at cost-index-refresh.yml:225 (warn-only, exit 0 verified) and is absent from freshness-heartbeat.yml's GATES list at lines 67-73; check-cost-index-orphans is absent too. I ran all seven heartbeat gates — every one exits 0 today, so nothing else covers it. basket.asOf = 2026-06-01 against _lastReviewed = 2026-08-05 reproduced. But the impact paragraph is out of date on two counts. The '8 → 16 in one week, nobody notified' decay narrative is refuted (see capacity-arithmetic). And 'within 33 days ingredient pages begin retiring [and orphan]' predates ADR-021: commit bc7b99285 built the terminal-page path — build-cost-index.mjs archives last-good state to data/cost-index-retired.json at the drop, build-cost-index-pages.mjs renders EN+ES terminal pages, and check-cost-index-orphans accepts retirement only with the published marker. The cliff is now a designed exit, not an orphaning.

title: The only hiring plan scopes a PM for the retired web-studio line, gates the hire on revenue that no longer exists, and would relieve none of the actual load
effort: 2 hours to retire; half a day to write the replacement scope
evidence: `docs/hiring/project-manager-scope.md` opens 'The first non-Don role at Muntin Digital' and describes the job as owning '/window/ submission' intake routing, '$499 audit delivery', the 'Care Plan Light monthly hygiene pass' across 'site + GBP + Yelp + Apple Maps', and Buttondown newsletter scheduling; it calls the company 'a one-person web studio in Silver Spring, MD' and says 'the studio is one operator-built voice.' The hire is gated on all three of '≥10 active Care Plan Light subscribers ($990/mo MRR floor)', '≥2 paid $499 audits per month, sustained 60 days', and '>15 hours/week on operations Don shouldn't be doing' (lines 11-19). But `CLAUDE.md` states the web-studio services line is retired and 301'd to `/studio/`, which is now the company page, and the company is 'product-only' — the Cost Index, free tools, and Muntin Ledger. Compensation is '$32–38/hour, contractor, 1099. Capped at 25 hours/week' = $3,467–4,117/month against zero revenue.
impact: Two of the three hiring triggers are unreachable by construction, so the doc guarantees the hire never happens — which is accidentally the right outcome for the wrong reason. The real risk is the opposite: if the founder ever acts on this doc, he spends $3.5–4k/month he does not have on a person scoped to a dead business, and none of the ~35 h/month I inventoried is PM work. Re-vendoring a snapshot, re-sourcing a NASS feed, running a backup drill, and writing a 3,200-word dispatch under a zero-invention fact gate cannot be delegated to a non-technical contractor.
rec: Retire `docs/hiring/project-manager-scope.md` the same way the course and services pages were retired — with a dated note pointing at what replaced it. If a first hire is ever affordable, the correct role is not a PM: it is 4–8 hours/month of a contract engineer with commit rights, a copy of the credential inventory, and a standing brief to clear the manual chore queue — which buys down the maintenance load AND the bus factor with the same dollar. Write that scope instead, and set its trigger to a revenue number the current business can actually produce.
note: Every quote reproduced from potentially-profitable/docs/hiring/project-manager-scope.md:1-19 — 'first non-Don role', the three-way trigger with the $990/mo Care Plan floor and the $499 audits, all naming the retired services line. The analysis is correct. The severity is not: this is a stale strategy doc in a repo with no hiring budget, no revenue, and no evidence anyone has looked at it since the retirement. The stated harm ('if the founder ever acts on this doc, he spends $3.5–4k/month') requires a founder who has $3.5k/month and has forgotten which business he is in. Low. Its real cost is that it is now published — the storefront repo is public (missed #3).

title: 29 externally-blocked founder items are 77 days old with none closed, and the runbook index that is supposed to make 71 runbooks findable is itself stale
effort: 90 minutes for the cleanup; 2 hours for the index gate
evidence: `runbooks/founder-todos.md` is dated 'Date opened: 2026-05-21' — 77 days ago — and carries F5 through F33 (29 entries) across sample assets, consent-gated items, deployment-gated verification, counsel review, and at-GA items. Only §1 (mailboxes/DNS) is marked DONE. The file's own closing rule is 'the file is meant to shrink … an entry that lingers because the founder forgot is the failure mode this file exists to prevent' — and nothing has shrunk. Launch-relevant entries still open: F9 (`runExtraction` two-network-hop never smoked on real infra), F11 (magic-link → Resend → handoff round-trip), F14 (the log drain that every alert rule depends on), F15 (NCMEC binding — `ncmecMatchStub` returns false), F16 (`/api/promises/last-verified.json` still empty, so `/promises` renders 'Not yet captured' for every promise per `runbooks/promises-last-verified.md:78`), F22 (counsel sign-off on the distributor wordmark strip). Two Pending DPAs (Intuit, Xero) sit in `docs/sub-processors.md:73-74`. Separately, `runbooks/INDEX.md` is headed 'Updated 2026-05-29' and 19 of the 71 runbooks are absent from it (verified by looping every `runbooks/*.md` against the index) — including `founder-todos.md`, `betterstack-alerts.md`, `promises-last-verified.md`, and `launch-plan-2026-11-13.md`. Worse, the index's very first 'Right-now operator tasks' row after the security checklist is `this-evening.md`, a 10-step deploy checklist pinned to branch `claude/app-audit-ux-refresh-eZPa2` at tip `9c378ce`, describing four commits waiting to ship — content that predates the current branch by months. `runbooks/first-deploy.md` still lists 6 Postgres migrations to apply; there are 59 in `infra/postgres/migrations/`. One small drift worth catching while you are in there: F18 records the security.txt `Expires:` as `2027-05-21`, but the file says `2027-05-10`, and its `Canonical:` is `https://muntin.digital/.well-known/security.txt` while F18's verification command curls `ledger.muntin.digital` — RFC 9116 requires the canonical URI to be where the file is actually served.
impact: The founder's own to-do system has stopped functioning as a queue and become an archive, so 'what is actually blocking launch' cannot be read off it. The runbook index — the single artifact whose job is to make 71 runbooks findable in a crisis — points a reader in a hurry at a months-dead deploy checklist as the top current task. During a real incident at 11pm after service, this is the difference between finding the right procedure and improvising.
rec: One 90-minute pass: delete every founder-todo that the 2027 launch deferral (ADR-020) has made irrelevant, mark the rest with a date and a one-line 'why still open', and demote the at-GA §7 items into a separate file so the active list is short enough to read. In the same pass, delete `this-evening.md` outright (it documents a shipped-or-abandoned branch), regenerate `INDEX.md` from the directory listing, and fix the security.txt Canonical/Expires drift. Consider a tiny gate that fails when a `runbooks/*.md` file is absent from INDEX.md — the repos already prove this pattern works (`check-idem-coverage`, `check-gate-coverage`).
note: Reproduced: founder-todos.md header 'Date opened: 2026-05-21' with only §1 marked DONE, last touched by any commit 2026-06-01; INDEX.md 'Updated 2026-05-29', last touched 2026-06-11; I looped every runbooks/*.md against INDEX.md and got 19 missing of 71; first-deploy.md lists ~6 migrations against 59 in infra/postgres/migrations/. The this-evening.md point is actually STRONGER than stated: it is not merely 'months dead' — `git rev-parse 1bb5dec` returns 'unknown revision', so INDEX.md's top 'Right-now operator task' points at a checklist whose four waiting commits are no longer reachable in the repository at all.

title: The cross-repo PAT is framed as the only path to automating the snapshot chore — a cheaper credential-free seam exists, and three other chores are equally automatable
effort: 3–4 days total, sequenced over a month
evidence: `docs/handoff/strategic-council-board.md` open item 9 records the cross-repo PAT as 'approved, not yet minted', and `Muntin-Invoice-Decoder/CLAUDE.md` states 'Full automation would need a cross-repo PAT (no workflow in either repo checks out the other) — a founder call, not added silently.' But both vendor scripts take their source path as an argument: `apps/api/scripts/vendor-cost-index.mjs:33` uses `process.argv[2] ?? resolve(here, "../../../../potentially-profitable/data/cost-index.json")`, and `vendor-cost-pressure.mjs:37-43` does the same for `pressure-rules.json` + `pressure-observations.json`. So the storefront's own `cost-index-refresh.yml` — which already holds `contents: write` on the storefront and runs Mon/Wed/Fri — could publish a small vendored export to a public path, and the product's existing `cost-index-snapshot-watch.yml` could curl it and commit with its own `GITHUB_TOKEN`. No cross-repo credential is minted at all. The one real obstacle is that `scripts/prune-dist-data.mjs` currently prunes `data/cost-index.json` out of `dist/` (its header, lines 5-22, explains why: 95MB of internal sources were shipping publicly), so the artifact must be an explicitly published export — and that script's own keep-rules (catalogued downloads + runtime-referenced paths) are exactly the mechanism for doing it deliberately. Ranked by hours saved per unit of effort, the other candidates: (2) a monthly cron that reds when `docs/warrant-canary.md`'s date exceeds 35 days — ~1 hour of work against a lapse that is currently at 88 days; (3) adding `check-cost-index-series-freshness` to `freshness-heartbeat.yml` — one line; (4) moving the 8 ADR-013 open-data fetches to GitHub Actions with repo secrets exactly as FRED/BLS/AMS already are (`cost-index-refresh.yml:56-79` proves the pattern works), which removes 8 of the 21 MANUAL entries and the single largest laptop-only dependency.
impact: The chore that has already caused one 42-day silent production outage (ADR-009 §7) and is 4 days from causing a second remains manual, and the stated blocker — a credential decision the founder has been deferring — is not actually the only path. Each unautomated chore is a recurring withdrawal from a capacity account that is already overdrawn.
rec: Do them in this order, cheapest-first: (a) wire the two missing gates into `freshness-heartbeat.yml` (1 hour); (b) add the warrant-canary staleness cron (1 hour); (c) publish a ~30KB vendored cost-index/pressure export through `prune-dist-data.mjs`'s keep-rules and have `cost-index-snapshot-watch.yml` curl-and-commit it — no PAT, no cross-repo checkout (1 day); (d) move the ADR-013 fetches into a scheduled workflow with repo secrets (1–2 days). Total ~3–4 days of work for roughly 15 founder-hours/month back, permanently, plus the elimination of two silent-dark failure modes.
note: The argv observation is correct at both cited lines (vendor-cost-index.mjs:33, vendor-cost-pressure.mjs:37-43) and the conclusion 'the PAT is not the only path' is right. The reasoning is needlessly elaborate and the auditor missed the one-line answer. Their proposal — publish a vendored export through prune-dist-data.mjs's keep-rules, then curl-and-commit it — is a day of work to route around a problem that does not exist: potentially-profitable is a PUBLIC repository (GitHub API `private:false`), so the private product repo's existing cost-index-snapshot-watch.yml can `actions/checkout` it with `repository:` and the default GITHUB_TOKEN, run both vendor scripts with argv paths, and commit. The Muntin-Invoice-Decoder CLAUDE.md claim 'Full automation would need a cross-repo PAT' is simply false, and the board's open item 9 ('PAT approved, not yet minted') should be closed as unnecessary rather than executed.

title: The storefront deploy is RED right now on real data drift, because the refresh workflow rebuilds data/cost-index-picker.js and then throws it away — third occurrence, hand-cleared twice, staging-list bug never fixed
evidence: `node scripts/check-all.mjs` on committed HEAD → `312 of 320 passed` and exit 1 (scripts/check-all.mjs:1009). Seven of the eight are `(idem)` injector drift expected outside the build chain. The eighth is not: `✗ Cost-index picker — grapefruit: dollarRef false != recomputed true`, from check-cost-index-picker.mjs:105, wired HARD into check-all at line 492. I proved it is stale committed data, not container noise: `node scripts/build-cost-index-picker.mjs` rewrites data/cost-index-picker.js (git shows it modified) and the gate then prints `OK — 81 ingredient(s)`. Root cause: .github/workflows/cost-index-refresh.yml:99 rebuilds the picker inside the keyed block, but the staging list at lines 302-312 omits `data/cost-index-picker.js` (it does include the sibling `data/cost-lockfloat.js`), and line 313 `git checkout -- .` then discards the rebuild. So every Mon/Wed/Fri the bot commits fresh cost-index data that the stale picker no longer matches — the 2026-08-03 and 2026-08-05 `muntin-cost-index-bot` commits are the ones that did it. check-all.mjs IS the Cloudflare `build.command` (wrangler.jsonc:159, joined by `&&`), so the deploy fails. `git log -- data/cost-index-picker.js` shows this has happened twice before and was cleared by hand each time: 0eb001af4 (2026-07-16) 'reconcile picker + revisions derived data to unblock deploy' and dea46ad34 (2026-07-28) 'regenerate lockfloat + picker stale after the main merge'. Nobody fixed the staging list. And nothing will report it: `grep -rn 'check-all' .github/workflows/` finds no storefront workflow that runs it, and freshness-heartbeat.yml runs only 7 hand-picked gates, none of them the picker.
impact: The auditor's #1 strength — 'the core data engine genuinely compounds unattended… _lastReviewed=2026-08-05 is direct evidence the loop is live' — measures the git repository, not muntin.digital. Data lands in main and the site does not rebuild. This is the 2026-07-30 lesson repeating verbatim, one level up: green bot commits are the presence of a shape, and the thing they are supposed to imply (a published site carrying today's numbers) is not happening. The only signal is a Cloudflare build-failure email, and the founder has made no human commit in either repo since 2026-07-31.
rec: Two lines, today. (1) Add `data/cost-index-picker.js` to the `git add` list at cost-index-refresh.yml:302-312 — it is the fix for all three occurrences and the same class of omission the comment at 296-301 already documents for cost-index-retired.json. (2) Commit the regenerated picker to clear the current red. Then close the structural hole: add a storefront workflow that runs the full injector chain + check-all on push and on a weekly clock, so the Cloudflare deploy stops being the only place 129 gates are ever truthfully evaluated.

title: Every production deploy step in deploy.yml is an `echo TODO` stub, the deploy audit-log step too, and the web target names a hosting provider the company does not use
evidence: deploy.yml:65-96: `Deploy api (wrangler)` → `echo "TODO(B-priv-6): wire wrangler deploy after cosign signing pipeline lands"`; the docling, extract and web steps are identical echoes with their real commands commented out. `Record deploy in audit log` at 97-100 is `echo "TODO: POST /v1/audit/deploys after the route lands"`. The web branch reads `Deploy web (Vercel)` with `pnpm dlx vercel deploy --prod` commented — while Muntin-Invoice-Decoder/CLAUDE.md specifies OpenNext → Cloudflare (`opennextjs-cloudflare build && wrangler deploy`) and runbooks/this-evening.md:12-16 lists the target as `muntin-web (Cloudflare Worker)`. Three sources of truth, two providers. The auditor cited this file at lines 20-31 and stopped before the body.
impact: The `environment: production` reviewer gate — cited in deploy.yml's header, in runbooks/two-person-prod-approval.md, and backed by a PGP-signed off-hours override procedure — guards a workflow that deploys nothing and records nothing. Real deploys happen from the laptop via scripts/deploy-api.sh and `pnpm --filter @muntin/web deploy:cf`, entirely outside the control. So there is no deploy audit trail at all, and the two-person control is not merely unconfigurable (the auditor's claim) but structurally bypassed by the actual deploy path. If any of this is ever shown to a design partner or an auditor as a shipped safeguard it is a false statement about security posture, and the Vercel reference means a reader cannot even determine where production runs.
rec: Either wire the real commands behind the gate or delete deploy.yml and say in one line where deploys actually happen. Do not keep a stub workflow whose header describes a control. Fix the Vercel/Cloudflare contradiction in the same commit, and when the audit-log route lands, make the laptop deploy scripts POST it — the trail has to follow the path deploys actually take.

title: potentially-profitable is a PUBLIC GitHub repository, publishing ~300KB of internal strategy including the launch-readiness self-assessment and contractor pay ranges
evidence: GitHub API: `Donwonmagic/potentially-profitable` → `private: false, visibility: public`, pushed 2026-08-06 (Muntin-Invoice-Decoder is `private: true`). I listed `docs/handoff/` through the public API and every file is readable: strategic-council-board.md (161,402 bytes), board-archive.md (140,666), founder-vision.md, ledger-audit.md, every-surface-map.md, retention-strategy.md, vb-world-class-roadmap.md. `git ls-files docs/handoff/ docs/hiring/` confirms all are tracked. docs/hiring/project-manager-scope.md publishes the contractor rate and the MRR triggers. wrangler.jsonc:159 excludes `docs` from `dist/` — so the exclusion keeps these off muntin.digital and creates a false sense that they are internal, while GitHub serves them to anyone.
impact: A company whose entire positioning is honesty about its own numbers has published, unintentionally, its frozen-feed roster, its capacity problem, its competitor reads, and its own record of what is not launch-ready — under its founder's real name, alongside a private product repo. Competitors named in the positioning (MarginEdge, Restaurant365, Toast) can read the roadmap. This is also the fact that dissolves the cross-repo PAT question the board has been deferring: a public source repo needs no credential to check out.
rec: Decide deliberately, then write it down — this company records decisions in ADRs and there is no ADR on repo visibility. Either (a) flip the repo private, which costs nothing today since the site is deployed from Cloudflare's git integration and no one forks it, or (b) keep it public as a build-in-public choice and move docs/handoff + docs/hiring into the private repo or a separate one. Do not leave it as an unexamined default. Whichever way it goes, use the public-source fact to kill board open item 9 (the PAT) rather than minting a credential.

title: GitHub silently disables scheduled workflows in a public repo after 60 days of inactivity — the exact mechanism the two absence alarms exist to defeat, unmentioned in either repo
evidence: potentially-profitable is public (above) and hosts both the data engine (.github/workflows/cost-index-refresh.yml, cron Mon/Wed/Fri 13:00) and the absence alarm (freshness-heartbeat.yml, cron Saturdays 12:00). GitHub disables `schedule:` triggers in a public repository after 60 days with no repository activity, notifying the owner once. `grep -rin "60 day|60-day|inactivity|automatically disabled|keepalive" .github/ docs/handoff/strategic-council-board.md` returns nothing; the same grep across Muntin-Invoice-Decoder/.github/ returns nothing. freshness-heartbeat.yml:12-20 reasons at length that 'the alarms that exist specifically for absence are the alarms that absence switches off' and cost-index-snapshot-watch.yml:15-21 repeats it — and both miss this. The only thing currently keeping the storefront warm is automation itself: all three August commits are `muntin-cost-index-bot` and `github-actions[bot]`, with zero human commits in either repo since 2026-07-31. And the board's own planning scenario at strategic-council-board.md:158 is 'a college course' — 'a year of coursework', which is six times the 60-day window.
impact: The single failure this company designed hardest against is the one it did not design against. If the founder goes quiet for a term, the crons stop, the Cost Index stops refreshing, and the heartbeat that would have told him stops in the same instant — silently, with one email among many. The public Cost Index then serves numbers frozen at whatever week he stepped away, which is the honesty failure the whole gate corpus exists to prevent.
rec: Confirm current behavior for this repo in Settings → Actions, then defend against it explicitly. Cheapest durable fix: give freshness-heartbeat.yml a step that makes a trivial repository write (or an issue comment) on every run so the inactivity clock never runs out — and put a comment on it saying WHY, since a future reader will otherwise delete it as pointless. Belt-and-braces: have the private product repo's Monday watch also `workflow_dispatch` the storefront's refresh, so two independent clocks in two repos with different visibility rules would have to fail together.

title: The warrant canary has never been published — there is no route that serves it and its signature fields are literal placeholders, so its staleness signals nothing to anyone
evidence: apps/web/lib/markdown.ts:124-128 names it explicitly: 'Known filename shape but no public route (warrant-canary.md, the runbooks/* files without a verify slug …): signal drop the link, keep the text.' `find apps/web/app -path '*legal*' -name '*.tsx'` returns dpia, transparency, transparency/[quarter], terms, ropa, privacy — no canary route. docs/warrant-canary.md:50-58 leaves 'Founder signature: [GPG signature attaches when the published version goes live]' and the key fingerprint as literal brackets, and states the published version 'lives at muntin.digital/ledger/canary' — a path that does not exist in the storefront repo either (`ls ledger/` → demo, index.html). The doc reads 'Last updated and signed: 2026-05-10' with a first-of-month cadence, so three updates are missed.
impact: The auditor used the 88-day lapse as a headline decay indicator in the posture and proposed a staleness cron for it in automation-debt. Both aim at the wrong thing. A canary with no reader cannot send the signal a canary exists to send — 'if it stops being updated, draw your own conclusions' requires someone watching. The real defect is a documented transparency control with no delivery surface, which is the same 'appearance of protection' pattern as betterstack-alerts.md and deploy.yml. Automating a reminder to re-sign an unpublished draft would add a recurring chore to an overdrawn capacity account for zero external benefit.
rec: Pick one and write it in an ADR. Either publish it — add the route, sign it once with a real key, and only then wire the monthly staleness cron — or move docs/warrant-canary.md to a `docs/designed-not-shipped/` folder with a dated header saying it is unpublished, exactly the way check-gate-coverage.mjs's UNWIRED registry handles a gate that does not run. The same pass should re-header betterstack-alerts.md and two-person-prod-approval.md; three controls share this defect and one convention should cover all of them.

title: There is no code path by which any customer can pay — revenue capability is zero, not just deferred
effort: 1 hour for the runway/ceiling decision; 2-3 weeks for billing when a date is set
evidence: `apps/web/app/(product)/settings/` contains appearance, audit-log, budgets, business-names, categories, data-map, export, integrations, labor, members, notifications, privacy, security — and no `billing`. A repo-wide grep for `billing/checkout` across `apps/web/app` and `apps/web/lib` returns ZERO callers; the endpoint exists only server-side at `apps/api/src/routes/billing.ts:118`. `apps/api/src/lib/stripe-tiers.ts:200-232` (`isEntitledForBeta`) fails OPEN when `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` is unset, so every org is entitled for free. `apps/web/lib/pricing-constants.ts:57-70` records that the $19/location founding rate has no SKU, no `priceIdForTier` branch, no `STRIPE_PRICE_*` field and no `trial_period_days`. ADR-020 (storefront `docs/editorial/decisions/ADR-020-*.md`) moved paid GA to 2027 with no date set and `apps/web/lib/launch.ts:52` has `LAUNCH_DATE_ISO = null`.
impact: Every month of operation is 100% cash outflow with a structurally zero-revenue front end. Even a founding-list member who wanted to pay today has no button to press. The infra obligation the code implies (see next finding) accrues from now until an undated 2027 launch — at ~$200/month that is another ~$1,000-2,000 of spend before the first dollar, on top of ~$1,400-2,800 already sunk since the 2026-01-01 sub-processor start dates.
rec: Do NOT build billing now — ADR-020 correctly de-urgentised it. Instead do the thing that is actually missing: write down the monthly obligation the code implies, compare it to your actual bank runway, and set a spend ceiling you will not cross before revenue exists. Then decide explicitly whether to keep the warm pool running while nobody is paying for it. When you do set the 2027 date, budget 2-3 weeks for the $19 per-location SKU + quantity + trial + a `/settings/billing` page.
note: Facts reproduced: apps/web/app/(product)/settings/ has 13 subdirs and no `billing`; grep for `checkout` across apps/web/app + apps/web/lib returns only two hits, both inside pricing-constants.ts comments — zero callers of apps/api/src/routes/billing.ts:118. isEntitledForBeta fails open at stripe-tiers.ts:236-238 when STRIPE_SECRET_KEY is unset. launch.ts:52 is `LAUNCH_DATE_ISO: string | null = null`. All true. But the severity is inflated: ADR-020 §Decision 4 (storefront docs/editorial/decisions/ADR-020-*.md:44-49) is a founder-signed decision that the billing build is 'de-urgentised, not cancelled', and stripe-tiers.ts:198-210 documents fail-open as an explicit founder call ('FREE PRIVATE BETA (founder decision, no Stripe yet)'). The auditor's own recommendation is 'Do NOT build billing now'. A critical finding whose remedy is 'do nothing' is a mislabelled decision, not a defect. What IS a defect — and the auditor missed it — is that even the tiers marked billable:true cannot charge: no STRIPE_PRICE_* appears in apps/api/wrangler.toml, so priceIdForTier returns undefined and billing.ts:150-158 answers `tier_unconfigured` 500. Revenue capability is zero across ALL four posted prices, not just the founding rate.

title: The deployed extraction pool costs ~$164/month at list price; every budget doc and the public cost page say $10-34
effort: 30 minutes to reconcile bills vs `fly machines list`; 1 hour to right-size and re-publish
evidence: `services/docling/fly.toml:29-31` sets `auto_stop_machines = false` and `min_machines_running = 2`; `:43-44` `cpu_kind = "performance"`, `cpus = 2`; `:56` `memory_mb = 8192`. The comment at `:25` claims the second warm machine costs "~$10/mo extra at current Fly pricing." At Fly list rates (assumption: ~$21/mo per performance vCPU, ~$5/GB-month RAM) one machine is 2x$21 + 8x$5 = $82/mo, and two are $164/mo — the comment is off by roughly 8x. `runbooks/first-deploy.md:21` budgets Fly at "$10-15 ... Two CPU-only Machines ... shared 1x CPU 256MB" — a machine class that is not what ships. `apps/web/lib/copy.ts:3286` publishes "Last month ran $37 of usage, so the real cost is about $34 a month right now. We republish this from each bill" — but `copy.ts:3246` says `Last reviewed: 2026-06-11` (56 days ago), and the warm pool only landed 2026-05-25 per the incident note in the toml, so that $37 covered ~6 days of it. Separately, `runbooks/first-deploy.md:136-160` still instructs the operator to deploy the *ephemeral* app and calls `services/docling/fly.toml` "STALE", while `scripts/deploy-docling-ephemeral.sh:24-55` is a hard-stop DO-NOT-RUN banner that names `services/docling/fly.toml` as the correct deploy — and no Fly Machines API caller exists anywhere in `apps/api/src`, so the per-job ephemeral design was never built.
impact: The largest recurring cash line in the business is potentially 8-10x its budgeted figure, and a public page tells prospective customers a cost number that is stale and structurally understated — on a page whose stated premise is that publishing the correction IS the brand. For a pre-revenue side venture funded from a salary, $164 vs $15 a month is the difference between rounding error and a real monthly decision.
rec: Tomorrow morning: `fly machines list -a muntin-docling-iad` and pull the last three Fly invoices. Reconcile against the toml. Then make an explicit call — with zero paying customers, a two-machine always-hot pool is buying cold-start protection nobody is currently experiencing. Consider min_machines_running=1 until a paying customer exists, and re-publish `/about/cost` from the actual July bill.
note: The Fly arithmetic is defensible: services/docling/fly.toml:43-44,56 is cpu_kind=performance, cpus=2, memory_mb=8192, and at Fly list rates (performance-1x/2GB=$31, performance-2x/4GB=$62 ⇒ ~$21/perf-vCPU + $5/GB) one machine is $82 and two are $164. The 'off by 8x' read of the :25 comment holds. BUT the auditor misread its own corroborating source. scripts/deploy-docling-ephemeral.sh:44-48 does NOT name the toml as shipped-correct at min=2 — it says the correct deploy is 'the NON-ephemeral app muntin-docling-iad (services/docling/fly.toml, min_machines_running=1)'. So there are THREE disagreeing sources, not two: runbooks/first-deploy.md:21 (ephemeral, shared 1x/256MB, $10-15), the deploy script banner (min=1 ⇒ ~$82), and the toml (min=2 ⇒ ~$164). $164 is the top of a range whose bottom is $82 and whose documented intent is $15; none is confirmed deployed. Report the range, not the point. Severity stays high — every reading is materially over the budget doc and over the public /about/cost figure — but the headline number is unestablished.

title: The public price posts per-month invoice caps that no code enforces — the only thing protecting the compute floor is a sentence on a marketing page
effort: half a day for either path
evidence: `apps/web/lib/copy.ts:3256-3260` publishes "Solo. $25/month. Up to 150 invoices/month." and "Team. $60/month. Up to 400 invoices/month." `apps/api/src/lib/stripe-tiers.ts:60-95` defines TierShape with `maxSeats`, `hasCockpit`, `hasStaffInvites`, `maxLiveRecipes` — and no volume field at all. A grep across `apps/api/src` for `invoice_quota|invoiceCap|maxInvoices|monthly_invoice` returns nothing. The only ingest throttle is `apps/api/src/routes/ingest.ts:130`: `rateLimit({ ip_per_minute: 60, org_per_minute: 600 })` — 600/minute is ~25.9M invoices/month, roughly 172,000x the posted Solo cap. `apps/web/lib/pricing-constants.ts` registers dollar amounts and their basis but has no field for volume, so `check-pricing-consistency.mjs` structurally cannot see this drift. `PLAN.md:111-113` carries a third, different tier table (Owner $24/100 invoices, Bookkeeper $59/400, Workshop $149/1500).
impact: The posted cap is the single lever that keeps a compute-heavy product priced like a note-taking app above its floor, and it exists only as prose. One high-volume multi-location operator on the $19 founding rate — which is posted with no cap at all — could consume arbitrary docling capacity. The floor holds today only because volume is zero, not because anything enforces it.
rec: Pick one: either (a) enforce the cap — a monthly counted-documents check at the ingest seam with a clear over-cap message, and add a `volumeCap` field to `pricing-constants.ts` so the gate can see it; or (b) delete the cap from the public copy and price/position for unlimited. Do not leave a posted limit that nothing enforces. Also reconcile or archive PLAN.md's contradictory tier table.
note: The enforcement gap is real: stripe-tiers.ts:62-98 TierShape has maxSeats/hasCockpit/hasStaffInvites/maxLiveRecipes and no volume field, and ingest.ts:130 is the only throttle. But the title's premise is false today. The 'Up to 150 invoices/month' strings render ONLY on the `!pre` branch of about/cost/page.tsx:97-136; isPreLaunch() (launch.ts:74-76) returns true whenever PUBLIC_LAUNCH !== 'launch', and PUBLIC_LAUNCH is not set in apps/web/wrangler.jsonc. In pre-launch the page shows chargeTitlePre/chargePreBody instead, which post no cap. A grep for '150 invoices|400 invoices|invoices/month' across every .html/.js/.json in the storefront returns ZERO. So nothing publicly posts a cap; this is latent launch debt behind one env flip, not a live exposure at zero volume.

title: Four public, unauthenticated storefront endpoints call a metered Google API with no caching and no spend cap
effort: 1 hour
evidence: `potentially-profitable/src/worker.js:648` puts `/api/gbp-lookup`, `/api/gbp-details`, `/api/psi`, `/api/crux-history` in the GET-allowed set with no session check. `:2244` reads `env.GOOGLE_PLACES_KEY` and `:2258` POSTs `https://places.googleapis.com/v1/places:searchText` with `maxResultCount: 5` and a field mask (`:2277-2312`) that includes `rating`, `userRatingCount`, `priceLevel`, `editorialSummary`, `serves*` — i.e. the highest-priced Places SKU tier (~$0.032-0.040 per call), despite the in-code comment claiming "cost per lookup is unchanged." `handleGbpLookup` performs NO cache lookup, and `:4077` notes the `AUDIT_CACHE` binding "isn't provisioned (i.e. today)" — confirmed by `wrangler.jsonc`, which binds only AUDIT_SNAPSHOTS and AUTH_SESSIONS. The only throttle is 30 requests/minute/IP (`:128`, `:684-692`). A grep for callers of these paths across every `.html` and `.js` in the storefront returns only `src/worker.js` and `src/lib/watch-checks.js` — no live page uses them; they are orphans of the retired web-studio line.
impact: One IP sustaining the rate limit is 43,200 calls/day ≈ $1,400/day at Places' atmosphere-tier pricing; a modest distributed scraper is multiples of that. Google Cloud applies no default spend cap. This is a dead surface — nothing on the site calls it — carrying an unbounded liability against a personal credit card. Whether it is live today depends entirely on whether `GOOGLE_PLACES_KEY` is still set in the Worker's secrets, which cannot be checked from here.
rec: Two commands tomorrow. (1) `curl https://muntin.digital/api/ping` and read `configured.places` / `configured.psi`. (2) If either is true: revoke the key in Google Cloud console and set a billing budget alert on that project regardless. Then delete the four route entries from `API_ROUTES` in `src/worker.js` — they serve no live page. If you want to keep them, put them behind the same session gate `/api/workbench/*` uses.
note: Reproduced end to end. src/worker.js:648 puts /api/gbp-lookup, /api/psi, /api/crux-history, /api/gbp-details in the GET-allowed branch with no session check (there is no global auth middleware — isOriginAllowed is called per-handler 42 times and handleGbpLookup at :2244 is not one of them). :2258 POSTs places.googleapis.com/v1/places:searchText with the atmosphere-tier field mask at :2283-2312 (priceLevel, editorialSummary, serves*, reservable) and maxResultCount:5. handleGbpLookup performs no cache read at all; wrangler.jsonc:322-325 binds only AUDIT_SNAPSHOTS and AUTH_SESSIONS, so the AUDIT_CACHE path at :4077 is dead. Only throttle is the 30/min/IP api tier at :684-692. Nothing in any .html or .js calls these paths — src/lib/watch-checks.js:104 only names them in a comment. Severity high is correct; exposure is contingent on GOOGLE_PLACES_KEY still being set, which the auditor correctly listed as unknown.

title: The entire acquisition strategy is organic content and there is no working analytics on either surface — CAC cannot be measured at all
effort: 2 hours to verify and wire; 1 day if standing up Plausible CE
evidence: The storefront loads `/assets/p.js` on 275 pages and initialises it with `plausible.init({ endpoint: '/api/event' })` (`index.html:71-72`). That proxy is `src/worker.js:479 → handlePlausibleEvent`, which forwards to a hard-coded `PLAUSIBLE_UPSTREAM = 'https://plausible.io/api/event'` (`:8699`) with no env override — the Plausible SaaS, not the self-hosted CE instance that `Muntin-Invoice-Decoder/docs/sub-processors.md` row 3 tells customers is used ("no data leaves our Fly instance"). On the product side `apps/web/app/api/event/route.ts:54` falls back to `http://plausible-ce.internal.invalid/api/event` and `apps/web/wrangler.jsonc` deliberately does not set `PLAUSIBLE_INGEST_URL`, so product beacons fail silently by design. Failures are swallowed on both sides (the storefront proxy returns 202 on any network error).
impact: The whole business model is content → funnel → founding list, and there is no instrument on the funnel. You cannot say which of 4.2M words of published content produced a single signup, so the implied CAC is not merely high — it is unknowable, and there is no basis to decide which content to keep making. Secondarily: either a Plausible SaaS subscription exists (an undisclosed sub-processor and an unbudgeted line) or it does not (in which case every beacon has been discarded upstream and the analytics have never worked).
rec: Decide in one sitting whether you have a plausible.io account. If yes: add it to `docs/sub-processors.md` and to the run-rate, and confirm events are landing. If no: either stand up the CE instance the docs already promise, or point the proxy at a real endpoint. Either way, before writing another article, get one number working end-to-end: sessions → /ledger/ → waitlist submit.
note: src/worker.js:8699 is `const PLAUSIBLE_UPSTREAM = 'https://plausible.io/api/event'` with no env override, forwarded at :8725 with the visitor's cf-connecting-ip as X-Forwarded-For; the catch at :8735-8739 returns 202 so failures are silent. Product side: apps/web/app/api/event/route.ts:54-56 defaults to http://plausible-ce.internal.invalid/api/event and PLAUSIBLE_INGEST_URL is absent from apps/web/wrangler.jsonc. The contradiction is sharper than the auditor stated: Muntin-Invoice-Decoder/docs/sub-processors.md:69 tells customers Plausible CE is self-hosted on the Fly tenant and that 'no data leaves our Fly instance', naming '/assets/p.js + the /api/event proxy' as the first-party path — the exact proxy that hard-codes the SaaS host and forwards the client IP to it. That is a sub-processor-disclosure defect, not merely an unbudgeted line.

title: The anonymous demo defaults ON against its own ADR, and the "$50/day worst-case bound" is a non-atomic KV counter
effort: 15 minutes for the flag; half a day for an atomic counter
evidence: `apps/api/src/routes/demo-extract.ts:95` disables the route only on the literal string `DEMO_ANONYMOUS_EXTRACT === "off"`. That var appears nowhere in `apps/api/wrangler.toml` — so unless it was set as a secret out of band, the live anonymous read is ON. ADR-007 §6 states the opposite: "the anonymous LIVE read is OFF until the first-try accuracy gate clears" and describes the flag as the gate. The budget breaker at `:186-197` does `kv.get(budgetKey)` → compare → and at `:352-359` `kv.put(budgetKey, String(budgetSpent + 2))` — a read-modify-write on eventually-consistent KV with no atomicity, so concurrent requests all read the same value and lose each other's increments; the per-IP counter at `:133-149` has the same shape. `docs/plans/try-anonymous-demo-plan.md:20` nonetheless calls it a "load-bearing worst-case bound: total anonymous spend cannot exceed ~$50/day." The cost constant `APPROX_COST_PER_RUN_CENTS = 2` (`:63`) is also ~4x the company's own published per-invoice figure (~$0.005), so the meter and the cost model disagree.
impact: Two exposures. Financially, the stated $50/day ceiling is not a ceiling under exactly the condition it exists for — a concurrent flood. Commercially the bigger risk is that an un-gated demo runs on accuracy the founder explicitly said was not good enough to show, so a bad first read burns a prospect permanently. Actual dollar exposure is bounded by fixed Fly capacity (the pool does not scale out), so a flood degrades service rather than the bill — which is arguably worse once a customer exists.
rec: Add `DEMO_ANONYMOUS_EXTRACT = "off"` to `apps/api/wrangler.toml` [vars] today and invert the check to require an explicit `"on"`, so the safe state is the default state. Then either move the two counters into a Durable Object (atomic) or stop describing $50/day as a bound in the plan and the ADR.
note: demo-extract.ts:95 is `if (env.DEMO_ANONYMOUS_EXTRACT === "off")` and the var appears nowhere in apps/api/wrangler.toml [vars] (grep across apps/, docs/, scripts/, .github/ finds it only in code, tests, ADR-007 and plan prose). ADR-007 §6 (docs/ux/decisions/ADR-007-...:103-110) states 'the anonymous LIVE read is OFF until the first-try accuracy gate clears', and docs/plans/first-try-reliability-roadmap.md:26 records the operator constraint 'not happy pushing the demo until it's the very best we can' with gate (a) still open. The KV race is real: read at :143-149 and :186-190, blind write-back at :354-358 with `String(budgetSpent + 2)`. Raising to high: this is the single clearest case in the domain of a documented safety decision that the shipped config does not implement, and a bad first read on the founder's own accuracy judgement is the acquisition asset burning, not a $50 line item.

title: Cost alarms are a manifest with no renderer, pointed at an app name that is not deployed
effort: 2 hours
evidence: `infra/cost-alarms.yaml:14-18` states plainly: "downstream tooling reads it to render the actual alarm rules ... The renderer is Lane 2 work; for now the file documents the contract." Nothing renders it. Its Fly alarm (`:96-108`) instructs `flyctl machines list -a muntin-docling-ephemeral-iad` — the ephemeral app that `scripts/deploy-docling-ephemeral.sh:24-55` declares broken/do-not-run and that no code ever spawns. Every alarm routes to `pagerduty_service: muntin-sre`, and a grep for pagerduty across `.ts`/`.sh`/`.yml` finds no integration. `runbooks/first-deploy.md:8` records "Last run: Not yet executed" — the cost table at `:19-26` was never validated against a real deploy, and its Cloudflare row says "Free $0" although `apps/api/wrangler.toml` uses Queues, Durable-Object-class ratelimit bindings and R2, which require the Workers Paid plan.
impact: The 2026-07-30 lesson repeated on the money surface: a document that describes protection is not protection. There is no mechanism by which the founder learns that a bill moved before the credit-card statement arrives — which is precisely how the docling pool went from a budgeted $10-15 to an implied $164 with nobody noticing.
rec: Skip the renderer. Spend 2 hours setting native spend/budget alerts in the four consoles that have them for free: Fly (spend alert), Google Cloud (budget alert — see the Places finding), AWS (billing alarm), Neon (usage alert). Then fix `first-deploy.md`'s cost table to match the shipped configs and mark it reviewed.
note: infra/cost-alarms.yaml:12-16 says outright that the renderer 'is Lane 2 work; for now the file documents the contract'; nothing reads it. Its Fly alarm at :90-108 targets muntin-docling-ephemeral-iad, the app scripts/deploy-docling-ephemeral.sh:24-55 declares DO-NOT-RUN. A grep for pagerduty across .ts/.sh/.yml/.mjs in both repos returns nothing outside this manifest. runbooks/first-deploy.md:8 is 'Not yet executed'. One thing to add that sharpens it: the Fly threshold at :92 is 60 machine-hours/day, derived as '2 services * 24h * 1.25' — but the shipped configs are 2 docling + 1 extract = 72 machine-hours/day, so the alarm as written would breach every single day if the renderer existed. The manifest was never reconciled against the tomls.

title: The two largest plausible cash lines — AI development tooling and CI minutes — appear in no cost document
effort: 1 hour to pull the bills; 1 hour to trim the nightly workflows
evidence: Across both repos, 763 of 925 commits are authored by "Claude" (`git log --format=%an`: storefront 274 of 343 since the 2026-07-05 history start; product 489 of 582 across 2026-06/07). Neither `runbooks/first-deploy.md`'s cost table nor `/about/cost`'s fixed list nor `infra/cost-alarms.yaml` contains any line for AI development tooling, which is the de-facto engineering department. On CI: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` declares 21 jobs (most `timeout-minutes: 5`, two at 10-15) that run per push, plus four nightly crons including `ocr-bench-nightly.yml:16,26` (60-minute timeout) and `mutmut-nightly.yml:25,35-36` (30 + 10 + 15 minutes). The product repo took 582 commits in roughly two months.
impact: If either repo is private, GitHub Actions on this cadence plausibly exceeds the free allotment by hundreds of minutes a month; on top of that the AI tooling subscription is likely the single largest recurring line in the business and it is invisible in every artifact that claims to describe what the company costs to run. Any "~$12-20/month" figure the founder reasons from is therefore not the real burn.
rec: Pull two actual numbers tomorrow — the AI tooling bill and the GitHub billing page's Actions minutes — and add them as first-class rows to a single run-rate sheet alongside Fly/Cloudflare/Neon/AWS/Resend. If Actions is material, cut the nightly OCR bench to weekly and gate `mutmut` on the Python paths changing; that is most of the spend for little lost signal at zero customers.
note: The commit-authorship counts are verifiable and the omission from every cost doc is real. But the dollar claim is inference stacked on an unknown the auditor itself lists: repo visibility is not determinable offline (remotes are github.com/Donwonmagic/potentially-profitable and /Muntin-Invoice-Decoder; no network from this container), and if either repo is public, Actions minutes are free and the entire CI half of the finding evaporates. 'Plausibly exceeds the free allotment' and 'likely the single largest recurring line' are both unsupported. This is a two-bills-to-pull note, not a finding with evidence; demoting to low.

title: Break-even is 9-13 paying locations — computable, achievable, and stated nowhere
effort: 2 hours
evidence: Inputs, all from code: fixed infra ≈ $164 Fly docling (`services/docling/fly.toml:29-56`) + ~$4 Fly extract (`services/extract/fly.toml:37-39`) + $5 Cloudflare Workers Paid (required by the Queues/R2/DO bindings in `apps/api/wrangler.toml`) + $0-19 Neon (`runbooks/first-deploy.md:22`; measured $0.84 for a partial month per `copy.ts:3288`) + $1-3 AWS KMS (`:23`; note `apps/api/src/lib/kms-client.ts:4-8` says the client is "PRE-FAB ONLY ... unused in production") + ~$2 domain + $8.25/mo amortised Apple Developer ($99/yr, `runbooks/launch-plan-2026-11-13.md:341`) ≈ **$185-205/month**, excluding AI tooling and CI. Variable cost per invoice ≈ $0.005 from the company's own table (`about/cost/page.tsx:57-63`). Net revenue after Stripe (2.9% + $0.30): $23.97 on Solo $25, $18.15 on a $19 location. Break-even: $200 ÷ $18.15 = **11.0 locations**, or ÷ $23.97 = **8.3 Solo accounts**. At 150 invoices/month the serving cost is $0.75, so contribution per location is ~$17.40 and the answer barely moves. Include AI tooling at $200/mo and it becomes 22 locations. Three months free (ADR-013) means each founding cohort contributes $0 for its first quarter.
impact: Not a crisis — the arithmetic works, and 11 restaurants is a plausible target for a founder who manages two of them. But it is nowhere written down, so the founder has no threshold to steer by, no answer to "can I afford to keep the warm pool hot," and no sense that the three-months-free term pushes break-even a full quarter past the 11th signup. Note also that this covers infra only; it pays the founder nothing.
rec: Write one page: fixed rows with real bills, variable per invoice, net after Stripe, the break-even count, and the date you would need to hit it. Pin it next to `/about/cost` so the public page and the internal sheet share one source. Then use it to make the warm-pool call in finding #2.
note: The negative claim is correct — I found no break-even sheet, no runway doc, and no contribution-margin figure in either repo. But the arithmetic inherits the contested $164 (see finding 2) and, more importantly, prices the wrong side of the offer. Solo's $23.97-net is not what a pre-launch signup will pay: apps/api/src/routes/waitlist.ts:95-103 defaults founding_member to TRUE on every capture, and data/sourced-claims.json#ledger_founding_offer_2026 commits founding members to '$19 a month per location for as long as they stay' with no cohort cap anywhere in ADR-013. For a single-location operator — the stated target — the realistic net is $18.15, not $23.97, so break-even is ~11 locations at the low infra estimate and closer to 22 at the high one, before the three-months-free quarter. The auditor computed both numbers but presented the $25 one as co-equal when no path in the code produces it for a pre-launch signup.

title: The monthly dispatch reaches almost nobody: 775 of 779 subscribe forms produce a `source` the broadcast filter excludes
evidence: `src/worker.js:8793` filters the Cost Index broadcast to `sub.source === 'cost-index'`. `src/worker.js:8746` defines the accepted set as `['footer','article-end','workshop-empty-state','window','cost-index']`, and `:8863` clamps anything outside it to `'footer'`. Counting the hidden inputs actually shipped in HTML: 613 pages post `value="footer"`, 162 post `value="cost-index-ingredient"`, 2 post `ledger-pricing`, 2 post `home-founding`, and only **2** post `value="cost-index"` (`cost-index/index.html:717` + the ES mirror). `cost-index-ingredient` is not in the allowlist, so all 162 ingredient pages — the deepest, highest-intent surface on the site — clamp to `footer` and are excluded. The generator and the receiver disagree in code: `scripts/build-cost-index-pages.mjs:2898` emits `source: 'cost-index-ingredient'` while the Worker has never heard of it, and no check-*.mjs gate references either constant (grep for `SUBSCRIBE_SOURCES|cost-index-ingredient` across scripts/ and src/ returns 3 lines, all of them the two definitions themselves).
impact: The company's entire strategy under ADR-020 is 'build the data-information business first' — 1,368 pages of content funnelling into an email list. The only broadcast that list ever receives is structurally wired to skip ~99.5% of the surfaces that collect it. Every footer signup and every ingredient-page signup gets a confirmation email and then silence, forever. This is the acquisition engine's one conversion asset, and it is disconnected at the seam. It is also the exact failure shape the 2026-07-30 audit named: a builder and a consumer that agree on a name in prose and disagree in code, with no gate binding them.
rec: Two lines today: add `'cost-index-ingredient'` (and `ledger-pricing`, `home-founding`) to `SUBSCRIBE_SOURCES` at src/worker.js:8746, and change the broadcast filter at :8793 from an equality test to a set membership over every source that opted into price content. Then write the gate that was missing: a check that every `name="source"` value emitted by any builder or shipped in any HTML is a member of `SUBSCRIBE_SOURCES`, and that every member is either broadcast to or explicitly listed as excluded. Before either, run the KV scan and find out how many active subscribers are sitting in the excluded buckets — that number is the cost already paid.

title: The dispatch silently drops every subscriber past the 90th and then marks the edition delivered
evidence: `src/worker.js:8789`: `const CAP = 90;   // Resend free tier is 100/day — stay under; larger lists need batching/queue.` The loop at `:8792-8801` increments `skipped++` past the cap and sends nothing. At `:8812` the success path stamps `cost-index:broadcast:<asOf>` in KV with a 120-day TTL as soon as `sent > 0`, so the edition is permanently idempotency-blocked from a retry. The workflow that fires it treats any 2xx as success, so the `skipped` count in the JSON body is never read by anything. There is no batching, no queue, no second-day continuation, and no alert. Note the interaction with the previous finding: today the cap is invisible because the audience filter already reduces the list to near-zero — fixing the source filter is exactly what will push the audience past 90 and make this fire.
impact: The newsletter is the only distribution channel a pre-revenue, content-led company has, and it has a hard ceiling of 90 recipients per edition that no one is told about. Growing the list past 90 produces zero incremental reach and zero signal that anything is wrong — the run stays green, the founder sees `ok: true`. For a business whose whole thesis is that the content compounds into a list that converts at launch, a silent ceiling on the list's only use is a growth stop disguised as a success.
rec: Make the cap loud before making it bigger: return non-2xx (or fail the workflow step) whenever `skipped > 0`, so the founder learns the edition was truncated on the day it happens. Then either move the send to a Cloudflare Queue that drains across days within Resend's 100/day, or price the Resend paid tier (~$20/mo for 50k) into the run-rate — it is the cheapest line in this entire audit and it unblocks the only asset the company is building.

title: The founding rate is an uncapped, perpetual discount that defaults ON for every signup, and the launch deferral made it a 12-month-longer commitment
evidence: `apps/api/src/routes/waitlist.ts:95-103`: `founding_member` is TRUE unless the submitter explicitly sends false/off/0/no — the comment says so outright ('Default ON: a bare hero capture (no checkbox) is a founding member'). The offer it entitles them to is registered in `data/sourced-claims.json#ledger_founding_offer_2026`: 'three months free, then $19 a month per location **for as long as they stay**', published on 30+ storefront pages per its own `used_in` array. `docs/editorial/decisions/ADR-013-commercial-posture-pricing-and-enterprise.md` sets the rate and parks enterprise; it contains no cohort cap, no expiry, no size limit, and no window — a grep for cap/cohort/limit/expire returns nothing. ADR-020 then moved launch from 2026-11-13 to an undated 2027, so the list accrues founding members for another 12+ months at no marginal commitment cost and no ceiling. Meanwhile `apps/web/lib/pricing-constants.ts:47-50` prices Solo/Team/Accountant on a `per_account` basis and founding on `per_location` — nothing in either repo resolves what a 3-location founding member pays (3×$19=$57) versus Team ($60/account, 2-5 operators), so the two systems are not reconcilable as written.
impact: Every dollar of break-even math the founder might do from the posted $25/$60/$150 tiers is wrong for the population that will actually be billed first. The realistic ARPU at launch is $19/location, ~24% below Solo, granted in perpetuity, to an unbounded cohort, starting after a free quarter. The deferral to 2027 is not cost-neutral: it is 12 more months of enrolling customers into the lowest price the company will ever charge.
